conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the decisive fork governing every nutritional decision?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Choose the least invasive route the gut can tolerate ("if the gut works, use it").

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is oral support used, and does it require a working gut?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Used when the patient can swallow safely
  • Requires a working gut: Yes.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is enteral (tube) feeding used, and does it require a working gut?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Used when there is unsafe/inadequate oral intake but a functional GI tract
  • Requires a working gut: Yes.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is parenteral (IV) nutrition used, and does it require a working gut?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Used when the GI tract is non-functional, inaccessible, or perforated
  • Requires a working gut: No.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Who is screened for malnutrition, how often, and how does MUST score (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Screen all inpatients on admission and outpatients at first appointment; repeat weekly for inpatients. The tool is MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool):
  • 0–2 for BMI (over 20 = 0; 18.5–20 = 1; under 18.5 = 2)
  • 0–2 for unplanned weight loss over 3–6 months (under 5% = 0; 5–10% = 1; over 10% = 2)
  • plus 2 if the patient is acutely ill and has had, or is likely to have, no intake for more than 5 days.
Total 0 = low risk, 1 = medium, 2 or more = high risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What criteria define a patient as malnourished (any one of)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• BMI <18.5
  • unintentional weight loss >10% in 3–6 months
  • or BMI <20 + weight loss >5% in 3–6 months.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What criteria define a patient as at risk of malnutrition (any of)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Eaten little/nothing for >5 days (or likely to for the next 5+)
  • poor absorption or high losses
  • increased needs from catabolism.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the daily nutritional targets (not severely ill, no refeeding risk)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Energy: 25–35 kcal/kg (lower if BMI >25)
  • Protein: 0.8–1.5 g/kg
  • Fluid: 30–35 mL/kg (+ extra for drains/fistulae).
Plus electrolytes, minerals, micronutrients, fibre.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are feeding targets adjusted after prolonged poor intake, or in severe illness?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days: start at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days, then increase if monitoring shows no refeeding problems
  • Severely ill or injured: start at no more than 50% of target and build up over 24–48 hours as tolerated.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What two conditions must both hold for enteral tube feeding to be indicated?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: (1) Inadequate or unsafe oral intake AND (2) a functional, accessible GI tract.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an NG tube — site, when used, and key points?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Site: stomach (nasal)
  • Use when: short-term (<4 weeks)
  • Key points: most common; allows bolus + hypertonic feeds; easily displaced.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an NJ tube — site, when used, and key points?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Site: jejunum (nasal)
  • Use when: short-term + delayed gastric emptying / reflux risk
  • Key points: reduces aspiration risk; post-pyloric placement can be difficult.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a PEG — site, when used, and key points?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Site: stomach (percutaneous)
  • Use when: long-term (≥4 weeks)
  • Key points: stroke, MND, Parkinson's, oesophageal cancer; placed endoscopically under antibiotic cover; usable 4 h after insertion.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a PEJ / jejunostomy — site, when used, and key points?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Site: jejunum (percutaneous)
  • Use when: long-term + high reflux/aspiration risk
  • Key points: permits early post-op feeding; more technically demanding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 4-week rule for feeding routes?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Less than 4 weeks → NG
  • 4 weeks or more → consider a gastrostomy (PEG).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the NG safety rule (NHS England) for confirming tube position?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Confirm position after placement, before every use, and after vomiting, retching or coughing — aspirate pH 1–5.5 on CE-marked pH indicator paper. If the pH is above 5.5, or no aspirate can be obtained, do not feed: get a chest X-ray reported by a competent trained assessor. Auscultation (the "whoosh" test), litmus paper and the appearance of the aspirate must never be used. Acid suppression can push gastric pH above 5.5. Giving a feed, flush or medication through a tube misplaced in the respiratory tract — misplacement not detected before use — is a Never Event.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does the duration of parenteral nutrition determine the access line?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• <14 days, no other central need → peripheral venous catheter (mind pH/tonicity)
  • <30 days → non-tunnelled central catheter
  • >30 days (long-term) → tunnelled subclavian line.
TPN is typically via a central line — the hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the complications of parenteral nutrition?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Line sepsis — the big one (daily catheter-site inspection)
  • thrombosis
  • refeeding syndrome
  • deranged LFTs / cholestasis
  • electrolyte and glucose disturbance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is trophic feeding and why is it used alongside PN?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Keep minimal enteral feeding alongside PN where possible → maintains gut function, reduces cholestasis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Carbohydrate load → insulin surge → rapid intracellular electrolyte shift → ↓phosphate (cardinal), ↓K+, ↓Mg2+ + expanding ECF volume. Thiamine demand spikes.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the cardinal electrolyte abnormality of refeeding syndrome, and the consequences?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Low phosphate is cardinal (with low K+ and low Mg2+). Consequences:
  • cardiac and respiratory failure
  • arrhythmias
  • rhabdomyolysis
  • seizures
  • coma
  • and Wernicke's encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency unmasked by the carbohydrate load.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the high-risk criteria for refeeding syndrome where ONE alone is sufficient (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• BMI <16
  • weight loss >15% in 3–6 months
  • little/no intake >10 days
  • low K+/PO4(3-)/Mg2+ before feeding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the high-risk criteria for refeeding syndrome where TWO are needed (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• BMI <18.5
  • weight loss >10%
  • little/no intake >5 days
  • alcohol or drug history (including insulin, chemo, antacids, diuretics).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is feeding started and built up to prevent refeeding syndrome (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Start at max 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg in extreme cases, BMI <14)
  • Build to full needs over 4–7 days.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What thiamine/vitamin and electrolyte management is needed in refeeding syndrome (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Thiamine 200–300 mg/day + vitamin B co strong — before and during the first 10 days
  • Replace K+, PO4(3-), Mg2+ as needed; do NOT pre-correct electrolytes before starting feeding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the tube-related complications of enteral feeding (NG vs PEG)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• NG: discomfort, sinusitis, erosions; bronchial misplacement (fatal if used)
  • PEG: stoma infection, peritonitis, dislodgement.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are blockage and infection prevented in enteral feeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Blockage: flush with water before and after every use
  • Infection: discard feed sets every 24 h.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is aspiration minimised during enteral feeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Nurse at ≥30° during and after feeding; use post-pyloric tubes for flat patients.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are GI symptoms (bloating, diarrhoea, nausea) managed in enteral feeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Slow the rate or switch to continuous feed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What bloods are monitored during feeding, and how often initially?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Bloods (daily until stable): U&Es, glucose, Mg, phosphate, LFTs/INR, calcium, albumin, CRP. Trace elements (Zn, Cu, Se) periodically on long-term PN.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What clinical and route-specific monitoring is done during feeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Clinical: weight, BMI, fluid balance, GI tolerance, tube/stoma site
  • NG: pH check before every feed
  • PN lines: daily site inspection for infection.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Is clinically assisted nutrition and hydration (CANH) a treatment or basic care, and what governs the decision?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: CANH is a medical treatment — not basic care. It can be withheld or withdrawn like any treatment, using the same consent framework. Capacity drives the decision.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a CANH decision made depending on capacity?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• A competent patient's refusal must be respected
  • If they lack capacity, decide in best interests (advance directives, MDT, family).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the goal of pre-operative management, and what are its key domains?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
It optimises the patient's condition before surgery to minimise perioperative risk, translating pre-operative assessment findings into action. Key domains:
  • consent
  • fasting
  • medication management
  • DVT prophylaxis
  • bowel prep
  • skin prep
  • and same-day checks.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does valid consent require under the Mental Capacity Act?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Capacity (understand, retain, weigh, communicate the decision)
  • voluntary (free from coercion)
  • informed (material risks, benefits, alternatives explained)
  • written consent on Form 1 for an adult with capacity having a procedure under general or regional anaesthesia or any procedure carrying significant risk (Form 2 = parental consent for a child; Form 3 = procedures where consciousness is not impaired; Form 4 = adult lacking capacity)
  • obtained by the surgeon or a trainee supervised by the surgeon.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the four components of capacity?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Understand
  • retain
  • weigh
  • and communicate the decision.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What did the Montgomery ruling establish about consent?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The patient must be told of all material risks — those a reasonable patient would want to know, or that this specific patient would consider significant. It replaced the old Bolam standard for consent; the surgeon must tailor the risk discussion to the individual and document the discussion, not just the signature.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is consent handled when capacity is lacking, for elective vs emergency surgery?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Act in best interests (MCA). Elective surgery: delay until capacity returns if possible. Emergency: proceed in best interests — consult next of kin (advisory, not legally binding) + document + consider an IMCA.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is pre-operative fasting necessary, and what does modern practice avoid?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Fasting prevents pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents (Mendelson's syndrome). Modern guidelines avoid prolonged starvation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 2-4-6 fasting rule?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Clear fluids (water, clear juice, tea/coffee without milk): 2 hours
  • Breast milk: 4 hours
  • Formula / cow's milk / solids: 6 hours.
These are minimums, not targets — prolonged starvation is harmful, and many UK units now allow clear fluids until an hour before surgery, or 'sip til send', particularly in children.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is carbohydrate loading, what are its benefits, and in whom is it avoided?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A pre-operative carbohydrate drink the evening before and up to 2 hours before surgery (an ERAS element). It reduces insulin resistance, anxiety and post-operative nausea. Avoid it in gastroparesis and in insulin-treated diabetes, where it may compromise glycaemic control; use it in other people with diabetes only where a local protocol allows.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are antihypertensives (ACEi, ARB) and diuretics managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Antihypertensives (ACEi, ARB): withhold the morning of surgery (risk of refractory intra-op hypotension with anaesthesia)
  • Diuretics: withhold the morning of surgery (risk of hypovolaemia + electrolyte disturbance).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are beta-blockers managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Continue — sudden withdrawal → rebound tachycardia / MI.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is metformin managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Metformin can usually be continued for a short starvation period (one missed meal) if renal function is adequate. Omit it on the day of surgery for major surgery or prolonged fasting, and use a VRIII if needed. It need not be stopped for iodinated contrast if eGFR is 30 or above with no AKI; withhold for 48 hours after contrast only if eGFR is below 30 or the patient has AKI. The concern is lactic acidosis with significant renal impairment.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is insulin managed perioperatively, and what must never be done?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Never stop insulin in type 1 diabetes — omission causes DKA. Continue the long-acting (basal) insulin at about 80% of the usual dose; omit or reduce short-acting and mixed insulin while nil by mouth, and follow the local protocol. A VRIII is used only if more than one meal will be missed, control is poor, or surgery is an emergency.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is warfarin managed perioperatively, and what is the target INR?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Stop 5 days pre-op and check the INR on the day; target INR below 1.5 for surgery. Most patients, including the majority with atrial fibrillation, do not need bridging — it increases bleeding without reducing thromboembolism. Reserve treatment-dose LMWH bridging for mechanical heart valves, VTE within the last 3 months, or previous thromboembolism during an interruption. For emergency surgery, reverse with prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K and discuss with haematology.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are DOACs managed perioperatively, and why the caution?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Stop 24 hours before low-bleeding-risk surgery and 48 hours before high-bleeding-risk surgery, stopping earlier if renal function is impaired — particularly for dabigatran, which is the most renally cleared. No bridging is needed because the half-life is short. Reversal agents exist (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for apixaban and rivaroxaban) but are restricted to life-threatening bleeding.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are antiplatelet agents (aspirin/clopidogrel) managed perioperatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Continue aspirin through surgery in most cases; clopidogrel is usually stopped 7 days before. Never stop dual antiplatelet therapy in a patient with a recent coronary stent without discussing it with cardiology — elective surgery is normally deferred until the mandated course is complete, and if surgery cannot wait, continue aspirin and restart the P2Y12 inhibitor as soon as haemostasis allows. Stent thrombosis is frequently fatal.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are the combined pill and HRT managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Combined oral contraceptive: stop 4 weeks before major surgery or surgery involving prolonged lower-limb immobility (VTE risk from the oestrogen); advise alternative contraception and restart once mobile
  • The progestogen-only pill does not need stopping
  • Oral HRT: consider stopping before major surgery with prolonged immobility, or switching to transdermal HRT, which does not carry the same VTE risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are long-term steroids managed perioperatively, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Continue the usual steroid and give perioperative cover — a patient on prednisolone 5 mg daily or more for 4 weeks or longer needs IV hydrocortisone at induction, continued until eating and drinking. HPA axis suppression means omission risks an adrenal crisis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are SSRIs/MAOIs managed perioperatively, and what is the risk?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Usually continue; avoid serotonergic drugs intra-op. Serotonin syndrome risk with pethidine, tramadol.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Who needs VTE risk assessment, and why does it matter?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: All surgical patients must have a VTE risk assessment on admission and after any change in clinical status (NICE). Hospital-acquired VTE is a major cause of preventable death in hospital.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanical VTE prophylaxis for surgical patients?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression, chosen according to the procedure and the patient (NICE). Stockings are contraindicated in peripheral arterial disease, peripheral neuropathy and severe leg oedema, and must be stopped if the skin marks, blisters or discolours. Add early mobilisation and adequate hydration.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH) started, and for how long?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Start 6–12 hours post-op, once haemostasis is confirmed. Continue for at least 7 days for general surgery, and 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is pharmacological VTE prophylaxis timed around a neuraxial block, and when is it withheld or dose-adjusted?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Do not insert or remove an epidural or spinal catheter within 12 hours of a prophylactic LMWH dose, and give the next dose no sooner than 4 hours after insertion or removal — otherwise there is a risk of epidural haematoma. Withhold for active bleeding or platelets below 50. If eGFR is below 30, use unfractionated heparin or a reduced LMWH dose.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the high-risk factors on the VTE risk assessment tool?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Malignancy
  • previous VTE
  • thrombophilia
  • immobility
  • BMI over 30
  • and major pelvic or lower limb surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the general principles of perioperative diabetes management?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Schedule first on the morning list where possible (minimises fasting time)
  • target blood glucose 6–10 mmol/L perioperatively
  • check capillary glucose at least hourly while nil by mouth and perioperatively, and check ketones if the patient is unwell or on an SGLT2 inhibitor
  • involve the diabetes specialist nurse or endocrine team.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is a VRIII (variable rate insulin infusion) indicated, and what fluid is it run alongside?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Indicated when the patient will miss more than one meal, control is poor, surgery is an emergency, or a type 1 diabetic has not had their long-acting insulin. Run it alongside a substrate fluid of 5% glucose + 0.45% NaCl + 0.15% KCl, and continue the long-acting insulin alongside it. Plain 0.9% saline is not used because it gives no glucose substrate (risking hypoglycaemia and ketosis) and no potassium, which insulin drives into cells.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a patient monitored on a VRIII, and when is it stopped?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Monitor glucose hourly on the VRIII and electrolytes 4–6 hourly. Convert back to subcutaneous insulin at the first meal — give the subcutaneous dose with the meal and continue the VRIII for a further 30–60 minutes before stopping it, or a type 1 diabetic will become ketotic.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Is routine mechanical bowel prep recommended, and when is it still used?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Routine mechanical bowel prep is not recommended for most colorectal surgery (no mortality or anastomotic leak benefit, and it causes dehydration). It is still used selectively — rectal surgery, where an intra-operative colonoscopy is planned, or before a defunctioning stoma. All colorectal cases receive IV antibiotic prophylaxis at induction.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What skin prep agent is preferred for SSI prevention, and how is hair removed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Chlorhexidine 2% in 70% alcohol — superior to povidone-iodine for SSI prevention (NICE). Hair removal: clippers NOT razor (razors cause micro-abrasions → ↑ SSI).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When are prophylactic antibiotics given for SSI prevention, and what else reduces SSI?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Prophylactic IV antibiotics at induction, before skin incision — earlier if a tourniquet is to be used. A single dose suffices for most operations; repeat only for long procedures or major blood loss, and do not prescribe a routine post-operative course. Also maintain normothermia (warm air blanket, warm IV fluids) and normoglycaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is ERAS, and for which surgery is it now standard?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery — a multimodal protocol across pre-, intra-, and post-operative phases. Reduces complications, length of stay, and costs. Now standard for colorectal, orthopaedic, and major abdominal surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the pre-operative ERAS elements?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Patient education and goal-setting
  • prehabilitation (exercise, nutrition, smoking cessation)
  • carbohydrate loading
  • avoiding prolonged fasting and bowel prep
  • anaemia correction — screen for anaemia, confirm iron deficiency with ferritin and transferrin saturation, then oral iron if there is time before surgery or IV iron if surgery is soon or oral iron is not tolerated
  • and VTE prophylaxis planning.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the intra/post-operative ERAS elements?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Short-acting anaesthetic agents
  • laparoscopic approach where possible
  • goal-directed fluid therapy (avoid over- and under-hydration)
  • epidural or regional anaesthesia to reduce opioids
  • early feeding (day of surgery or day 1)
  • early mobilisation
  • avoid NGT, urinary catheter and drains if not required.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is checked at "Sign in" (before induction) on the WHO checklist?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Patient identity + consent confirmed
  • site marked
  • allergies
  • anaesthetic equipment checked
  • pulse oximetry working.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is checked at "Time out" (before skin incision) on the WHO checklist?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• All team members introduced
  • patient/site/procedure confirmed
  • antibiotic given
  • imaging displayed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is checked at "Sign out" (before leaving theatre) on the WHO checklist?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Swab/instrument/sharps count correct
  • specimens labelled
  • equipment problems noted
  • recovery plan discussed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist for, and how strong is the evidence?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: It is mandatory in all NHS theatres. It improves team communication and reduces never-events such as wrong-site surgery. The size of its effect on mortality is debated — later population-level studies have not reproduced the large reductions reported in the original before-and-after study.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the decisive fork that governs the entire acute GI bleed workup, and what divides it?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Upper vs lower, divided by the ligament of Treitz.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Define an upper GI bleed by site, and how is it triaged?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Oesophagus, stomach or duodenum (proximal to the ligament of Treitz). Triaged to endoscopy (OGD).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Define a lower GI bleed by site, and how is it triaged?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Below the ligament of Treitz. Triaged to imaging / colonoscopy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the safety rule for a haemodynamically unstable patient with a large fresh PR bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: They have an upper GI bleed until proven otherwise (a brisk upper bleed transits fast and presents as fresh rectal blood).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What vocabulary points to an upper vs a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Haematemesis / "coffee-ground" vomit + melaena → upper
  • Haematochezia (fresh PR blood) → usually lower.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the "resuscitate first" universal principle in an acute GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Unstable bleeds need urgent resuscitation, wide-bore IV access and blood products until stable; activate the major haemorrhage protocol
  • Restrictive transfusion (Hb <70 g/L, target 70–90) unless massive haemorrhage or instability — take particular care not to over-transfuse a variceal bleed, as this raises portal pressure
  • Correct coagulopathy: platelets if actively bleeding with a count below 50; prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K for warfarin; stop a DOAC and discuss with haematology
  • Continue low-dose aspirin taken for secondary prevention once haemostasis is achieved (NICE).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the "FBC trap" in an acute GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Acute bleeds may NOT initially show anaemia — Hb concentration lags (takes time to haemodilute), so a normal Hb never reassures in an acute bleed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does the urea:creatinine ratio help localise a GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A raised urea:creatinine ratio points to an upper source (digested blood is a protein load absorbed in the gut, so a raised urea with normal creatinine points to an upper GI source).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the causes of an upper GI bleed, in rank order?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Peptic ulcer disease (commonest)
  • then gastritis/duodenitis/oesophagitis
  • oesophageal varices
  • Mallory-Weiss tear
  • malignancy
  • and vascular lesions (angiodysplasia, Dieulafoy).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the decisive sub-fork in an upper GI bleed, and why does it matter?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Variceal vs non-variceal — it changes the drugs entirely.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the clinical features of an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Haematemesis
  • "coffee-ground" vomit
  • melaena (black, tarry, sticky and offensive-smelling — digested blood; distinguish from the dry, matt-black, non-offensive stool of oral iron or bismuth)
  • epigastric pain (ulcer)
  • and signs of chronic liver disease (varices).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What bloods are sent in an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• FBC
  • U&Es
  • LFTs
  • coagulation screen
  • group & save / crossmatch
  • VBG + lactate.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the urea clue in an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Urea is disproportionately raised relative to creatinine — digested blood is a protein load absorbed in the gut, so a raised urea with normal creatinine points to an upper GI source.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Glasgow-Blatchford score (GBS) — when is it used and its purpose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Used pre-endoscopy. A score of 0 = very low risk → consider outpatient / early discharge (uses Hb, urea, SBP, HR, melaena, syncope, liver disease, heart failure).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Rockall score — when is it used and its purpose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Used post-endoscopy. Predicts rebleeding and mortality (age, shock, comorbidity, diagnosis, endoscopic stigmata).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the OGD timing in an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Unstable severe bleed → endoscopy immediately after resuscitation (in practice within 2 hours of optimal resuscitation)
  • All other patients, including stable suspected variceal bleeds, → within 24 hours of admission (NICE).
The trigger is haemodynamic instability, not the aetiology.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a non-variceal upper GI bleed managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Endoscopic haemostasis — clips or thermal coagulation. PPI AFTER endoscopy, not before (NICE) — then IV PPI (omeprazole 80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/h for 72 h post-haemostasis).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is a PPI given in a non-variceal upper GI bleed, and what is the regimen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: PPI AFTER endoscopy, not before (NICE) — IV PPI (omeprazole 80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/h for 72 h post-haemostasis).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the three-part bundle for a variceal upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Terlipressin IV + prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics, both at presentation, + urgent endoscopic therapy — band ligation for oesophageal varices, injection of cyanoacrylate glue for gastric varices (NICE). TIPS if bleeding is not controlled endoscopically.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the management if endoscopy fails to control an upper GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: CT mesenteric angiography to identify/control the source → guide embolisation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the causes of a lower GI bleed, in rank order?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Diverticular disease (commonest)
  • then benign anorectal disease (haemorrhoids, fissure)
  • colitis (IBD, infective or ischaemic)
  • colorectal neoplasia
  • angiodysplasia and post-polypectomy bleeding.
In a substantial minority no source is ever identified.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Are diverticular bleeds painful, and how does this differ from diverticulitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Diverticulosis is the commonest cause; diverticular bleeds are often painless, but bleeds from diverticulitis can be painful.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is angiodysplasia, where do AVMs form, and what bleeds does it cause?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The most common vascular abnormality of the GI tract; lesions form most often in the caecum and ascending colon. It is an important cause of obscure and small-bowel bleeding, particularly in older patients.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does angiodysplasia present and behave?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Presents as painless occult or recurrent PR bleeding; usually stops spontaneously but frequently recurs.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the associations of angiodysplasia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Aortic stenosis (Heyde's syndrome)
  • chronic renal failure
  • von Willebrand disease.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is angiodysplasia managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Argon plasma coagulation (APC); capsule endoscopy preferred for small-bowel lesions.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is Heyde's syndrome?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Aortic stenosis + angiodysplasia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the character of haematochezia suggest about the cause of a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Haematochezia (fresh/maroon PR blood); painless suggests diverticular/angiodysplasia, painful suggests colitis/ischaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What examination do all patients with a lower GI bleed need, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A DRE + proctoscopy — to exclude a bedside-treatable anorectal source (haemorrhoids).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the risk factors for an adverse outcome in a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Haemodynamic instability
  • ongoing haematochezia
  • age >60
  • creatinine >150
  • significant comorbidities.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the Oakland score do in a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Stratifies whether outpatient management is feasible (age, sex, previous LGIB admissions, PR findings, HR, SBP, Hb). A score of 8 or less identifies patients who can be discharged for outpatient investigation (BSG).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What bloods are sent as a minimum in a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: FBC, U&Es, LFT, clotting and Group & Save as a minimum; stool cultures to exclude infective causes.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the stability-driven imaging fork for a stable (~80%) lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mild & self-limiting → colonoscopy once stable + bowel-prepped (diagnostic + therapeutic).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the stability-driven imaging fork for an unstable lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Resuscitate + correct coagulopathy + major haemorrhage protocol. Exclude an upper source first with OGD if the history suggests one, then urgent CT angiogram BEFORE any endoscopic therapy → permits IR embolisation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What if colonoscopy is negative in a lower GI bleed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Do an OGD to look for an upper source; if still inconclusive → capsule endoscopy or RBC scintigraphy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What proportion of lower GI bleeds settle spontaneously, and what does this allow?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: ~80% settle spontaneously — stable, low-risk young patients in whom bleeding has stopped can be discharged for outpatient investigation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the management options for a lower GI bleed (endoscopic, IR, surgery)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Endoscopic therapy (clips, thermal, APC for angiodysplasia, band ligation)
  • IR embolisation (via CT angiogram) for ongoing bleeding not controlled endoscopically
  • surgery = last resort (unstable despite resuscitation, or failed endoscopic/IR control).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is an unstable lower GI bleed managed in terms of pathway, and what proportion settle?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Unstable lower bleed → CT angiogram before endoscopy → IR embolisation. Overall ~80% of lower GI bleeds settle spontaneously, but an unstable bleed needs active intervention.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Erosive gastritis and duodenitis are a common cause of upper GI bleeding. Name the two eponymous stress ulcers and their triggers.
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Curling's ulcer = severe burns (gastric mucosal ischaemia)
  • Cushing's ulcer = head injury / raised ICP (vagal overstimulation → excess acid).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Who should receive stress ulcer prophylaxis to prevent GI bleeding, and with what?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The critically ill — major burns, head injury, mechanical ventilation for over 48 hours, coagulopathy. Give a PPI or an H2-receptor antagonist.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the initial priority and decisive fork in the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Sudden onset of severe abdominal pain. Initial priority: A–E, obs, resuscitate first, then take a history. The decisive fork: urgent intervention now (bleed/perforation/ischaemia) vs further investigation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the three "must not miss" emergencies in the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Acute bleeding (ruptured AAA, or a ruptured ectopic pregnancy in a woman of reproductive age)
  • perforated viscus
  • and ischaemic bowel.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: For acute bleeding: worst cause, cardinal clue, key bloods, and definitive investigation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Worst cause: ruptured AAA → vascular team; in a woman of reproductive age, a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
  • Cardinal clue: hypovolaemic shock (tachy, hypotension, pale).
  • Key blood: ↓ Hb.
  • Definitive Ix: CT angiography if haemodynamically stable — if unstable, do not delay for imaging, transfer immediately to the vascular unit.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: For perforated viscus: worst causes, cardinal clue, key bloods, and definitive investigation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Worst causes: peptic ulcer, diverticulitis, perforated appendix, obstructing colorectal cancer.
  • Cardinal clue: peritonism — involuntary guarding, percussion tenderness and pain on coughing (elicit by percussion or cough, not deep palpation and release) — progressing to a rigid abdomen.
  • Key bloods: ↑ WCC/CRP.
  • Definitive Ix: CT abdomen/pelvis; an erect CXR is a quick screen for free air but a normal film does not exclude perforation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: For ischaemic bowel: worst cause, cardinal clue, key bloods, and definitive investigation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Worst cause: acute mesenteric ischaemia.
  • Cardinal clue: pain out of proportion to examination.
  • Key bloods: ↑ lactate, metabolic acidosis — but lactate rises late, so a normal lactate does not exclude it.
  • Definitive Ix: CT angiography, done on clinical suspicion.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for right hypochondriac pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Gallstones
  • cholangitis
  • hepatitis
— plus cardiac/lung referred pain (always consider the chest).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for epigastric pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Oesophagitis
  • peptic/perforated ulcer
  • pancreatitis
  • MI (referred).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for left hypochondriac pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Gastritis / peptic ulcer
  • pancreatitis
  • splenic infarct or rupture (trauma, glandular fever).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for right/left lumbar pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Ureteric colic
  • pyelonephritis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for umbilical pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Appendicitis (early)
  • mesenteric lymphadenitis
  • Meckel's.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for right iliac fossa pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Appendicitis
  • Crohn's
  • caecal obstruction
  • ovarian cyst
  • ectopic pregnancy
  • hernia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for hypogastric pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Urinary retention, cystitis
  • ectopic pregnancy, PID, ovarian torsion
  • testicular torsion (always examine the external genitalia in a male with lower abdominal pain) and strangulated hernia (always examine the hernial orifices).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key differentials for left iliac fossa pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Diverticulitis
  • UC
  • constipation
  • ovarian cyst.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the distinguisher for biliary colic vs acute cholecystitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Biliary colic: post-fatty meal; no fever, normal markers.
  • Acute cholecystitis: Murphy's sign +ve, fever, ↑ CRP.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the distinguisher for ascending cholangitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Charcot's triad: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the distinguisher for pancreatitis (hepatobiliary table)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Epigastric → back; ↑ amylase or lipase (>3× ULN), with lipase preferred where available.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the lower GI differentials and their distinguishing features?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Appendicitis — central → RIF, anorexia, low-grade fever, Rovsing's sign.
  • Diverticulitis — constant LIF pain, usually severe, with fever and ↑ WCC/CRP.
  • Obstruction — central colicky pain, no bowels/flatus, tinkling sounds.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How do peptic ulcers present, and how do duodenal vs gastric ulcers relate to eating?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Peptic ulcer — epigastric, NSAID/alcohol history.
  • Duodenal ulcer: relieved by eating.
  • Gastric ulcer: worsened by eating.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the medical mimics of an acute abdomen, and how should they be handled?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• MI (epigastric referred pain; always do an ECG)
  • DKA
  • Addisonian crisis
  • porphyria, lead poisoning
  • lower-lobe pneumonia.
Treat the medical cause first rather than rushing to theatre — but note DKA can itself be precipitated by an intra-abdominal cause: pain that persists after the DKA is corrected needs re-examination and imaging.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the urological differentials and their distinguishing features?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Renal colic — loin → groin, severe/intermittent, haematuria.
  • Pyelonephritis — loin pain, fever/rigors.
  • Urinary retention — suprapubic, male/BPH.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is mandatory in all reproductive-age women with an acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A urine pregnancy test — in every woman of childbearing age, regardless of contraception, sterilisation, reported sexual history or a "normal" last period. A positive test with abdominal pain and tenderness is an ectopic until proven otherwise.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does an ectopic pregnancy present?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Pelvic or iliac fossa pain with a positive pregnancy test
  • ± amenorrhoea
  • ± PV bleeding
  • ± shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or collapse.
Atypical presentation is common — a normal period history does not exclude it.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the other gynaecological differentials in the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Ovarian cyst torsion
  • PID.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the vascular differentials and their distinguishing features?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Ruptured AAA — central → back, collapse, pulsatile mass.
  • Mesenteric ischaemia — AF/CVD history, pain out of proportion to examination, ↑ lactate (which rises late, so a normal lactate does not exclude it).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What investigations make up the acute abdomen work-up?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Urine dip + MC&S (interpret with caution — sterile pyuria and haematuria occur in appendicitis and pelvic inflammation, and a positive dip does not exclude a surgical cause)
  • pregnancy test in every woman of childbearing age
  • ECG (exclude MI)
  • ABG/VBG (lactate, though normal does not exclude ischaemia)
  • FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, amylase or lipase (lipase preferred), INR, calcium
  • erect CXR
  • CT abdomen/pelvis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the initial management bundle for the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• A–E; alert seniors early in the unwell patient.
  • NBM if surgery likely or obstruction.
  • NG tube if obstruction.
  • IV fluids if hypovolaemia.
  • Score NEWS2 and screen for sepsis — blood cultures and lactate first, then broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour in high-risk sepsis, escalating in parallel because source control is the definitive treatment.
  • Analgesia early and titrated (IV morphine with an anti-emetic) — do not withhold opioids for fear of masking signs.
  • VTE assessment + LMWH prophylaxis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does pain out of proportion to examination signify until proven otherwise?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mesenteric ischaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the three classic named signs and their conditions?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Charcot's triad = cholangitis.
  • Murphy's = cholecystitis.
  • Rovsing's = appendicitis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the classic pain-migration patterns in the acute abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Appendicitis: umbilicus → RIF.
  • Renal colic: loin → groin.
  • AAA/pancreatitis: → back.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the ulcer food rule, and what do the key bloods indicate?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Duodenal = relieved by food; gastric = worsened by food. Key bloods:
  • amylase or lipase >3× ULN supports pancreatitis
  • ↑ lactate suggests ischaemia (normal does not exclude it)
  • ↓ Hb = bleed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is acute appendicitis, where is the appendix, what is the peak age, and which group is the can't-miss high-risk group?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Inflammation of the appendix — a blind-ended tube from the caecum where the three taeniae coli converge.
  • Peak age is the second decade (~10–20 years, into the early 20s)
  • children are the can't-miss high-risk group (atypical presentation + high perforation risk).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the decisive cascade in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Luminal obstruction → trapped secretions → infection & inflammation → gangrene → rupture → peritonitis. The timeline drives urgency.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the causes of luminal obstruction in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Faecolith (compacted faecal stone — classic)
  • lymphoid hyperplasia (commoner in younger patients, post-viral)
  • undigested seeds/impacted stool
  • caecal tumour (the can't-miss cause in older patients).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the cardinal pain pattern of appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Starts central/peri-umbilical (dull, poorly localised — visceral midgut pain) → migrates to RIF (sharp, well localised — parietal peritoneal inflammation). Worse on coughing / speed bumps.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the significance of vomiting timing relative to pain in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Pain-first = appendicitis order
  • vomiting-first = gastroenteritis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the key symptoms of appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Pain — central → RIF migration (key feature)
  • vomiting after pain
  • anorexia, nausea
  • constipation > diarrhoea (pelvic appendicitis → rectal irritation / loose stool).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the examination findings in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• McBurney's point tenderness
  • percussion and cough tenderness with guarding → peritonism (preferred to eliciting rebound — kinder and no less useful)
  • RIF mass → appendiceal abscess
  • sepsis signs in severe cases (tachycardia, hypotension)
  • Rovsing's sign (LIF palpation → RIF pain)
  • psoas sign (RIF pain on right hip extension → retrocaecal appendix).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is Rovsing's sign?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: LIF palpation → RIF pain.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the psoas sign, and what does it indicate?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: RIF pain on right hip extension → a retrocaecal appendix.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why are children atypical and high-risk in appendicitis, and what should be examined?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• They often present with diarrhoea, urinary symptoms, or left-sided pain.
  • Examine GI, urinary AND genitals in all boys (exclude testicular torsion).
  • A child under 6 with symptoms for more than 48 hours is at high risk of having already perforated — escalate urgently to the surgical team.
Active observation with serial examination is for children with a short history and equivocal findings, not for this group.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the adult differentials for RIF pain?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Gynaecological — ovarian torsion (time-critical, and a negative pregnancy test does not exclude it), ovarian cyst rupture, ectopic pregnancy, PID
  • renal — ureteric colic, UTI, pyelonephritis
  • GI — Crohn's, Meckel's diverticulum, diverticular disease
  • urological — testicular torsion, epididymo-orchitis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the paediatric differentials for appendicitis, and which is the commonest mimic?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Mesenteric adenitis — inflamed mesenteric nodes, often post-URTI/tonsillitis; the commonest paediatric mimic. Also gastroenteritis, constipation, intussusception, UTI, and testicular torsion (boys).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: If the appendix is normal at operation, what should be inspected and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Inspect the distal ileum for an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum — a congenital blind-ended diverticulum ~60 cm from the ileocaecal valve that can inflame, rupture, or cause volvulus/intussusception.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Is appendicitis a clinical or an imaging diagnosis in UK practice?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Primarily clinical — but imaging is used increasingly because operating on clinical grounds alone leaves a high negative appendicectomy rate, highest in women of childbearing age.
  • A classical history with localised RIF peritonism and raised inflammatory markers may go straight to theatre
  • image before operating if the presentation is atypical or equivocal, and in particular in women of childbearing age, children, older patients and pregnancy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What blood tests are used in appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: FBC + CRP + G&S: neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis; ↑ CRP. G&S if surgical intervention is planned.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the role of urine dip and pregnancy test in suspected appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Urinalysis to exclude renal/urological causes.
  • A urine pregnancy test is mandatory in every woman of childbearing age before any decision to operate — a negative test excludes ectopic pregnancy.
  • If positive, urgent gynaecological assessment and pelvic ultrasound are needed.
  • Serum hCG is used where the urine test is equivocal or quantification is needed.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is imaging used in suspected appendicitis, and what is preferred in women, children and pregnancy?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• In women, ultrasound first: transabdominal graded-compression USS to assess the appendix, plus pelvic/transvaginal USS to assess the adnexa (torsion, cyst accident, tubo-ovarian pathology).
  • USS is preferred over CT in children (avoid radiation).
  • CT if the diagnosis remains unclear.
  • In pregnancy, USS first and CT avoided (fetal radiation), with non-contrast MRI next if USS is inconclusive.
A non-visualised appendix on USS does not exclude appendicitis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the gold-standard surgical management of appendicitis, and what is the approach in pregnancy?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Laparoscopic appendicectomy — the gold standard; inspect the whole abdomen for other pathology.
  • In pregnancy, laparoscopic appendicectomy is now considered safe in all trimesters (RCOG) and is increasingly preferred; an open/muscle-splitting (Lanz) approach remains an alternative, especially in advanced pregnancy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is an appendiceal mass managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• IV antibiotics and conservative management.
  • Interval appendicectomy is no longer routine — it is reserved for recurrent or persistent symptoms.
  • In older patients arrange interval colonic imaging (CT and/or colonoscopy) to exclude an underlying caecal or appendiceal malignancy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does a pelvic abscess present after appendicectomy, and how is it managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Typically days after appendicectomy for a perforated appendix: swinging pyrexia, diarrhoea, tenesmus and mucus per rectum, with a boggy tender mass on digital rectal examination (not usually palpable abdominally).
  • Confirmed on CT; managed with IV antibiotics and image-guided drainage.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the status of antibiotic-only management for appendicitis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: An established option for selected adults with uncomplicated appendicitis — no perforation, no abscess and no appendicolith. Appendicectomy remains the definitive treatment and is preferred for complicated appendicitis; a substantial minority treated with antibiotics recur within a year and come to surgery, so this belongs in the consent discussion.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the most serious complication of appendicitis, and what are its signs?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Perforation: peritoneal contamination → generalised peritonitis, especially in children with delayed presentation (>48 h). Signs:
  • sudden pain relief then worsening
  • rigid abdomen
  • sepsis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an appendiceal mass (complication), and how does a pelvic abscess complication present?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Appendiceal mass — omentum and small bowel wall off the appendix, giving a palpable RIF mass.
  • Pelvic abscess — swinging pyrexia, diarrhoea, tenesmus and mucus per rectum with a boggy tender mass on PR; CT-confirmed; IV antibiotics and image-guided drainage.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the other complications of appendicitis besides perforation, mass and pelvic abscess?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Surgical site infection
  • stump appendicitis (rare — if insufficient appendix removed).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why does an obstructing tumour matter in an older patient with appendicitis, and what does sending the appendix for histopathology actually achieve?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• In older patients an obstructing caecal or appendiceal tumour must be considered, though a faecolith is still the commonest cause at any age.
  • The appendix is always sent for histopathology — this detects an appendiceal neoplasm (most often a neuroendocrine/carcinoid tumour).
It does not exclude a caecal tumour: that needs interval colonic imaging or colonoscopy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the purpose of pre-operative assessment, and what is the ideal timing?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: To identify comorbidities that risk complications during anaesthesia, surgery or recovery. Timing: far enough before surgery to identify and optimise comorbidities and to complete any further tests or referrals.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does urgency dictate the depth of pre-operative optimisation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Elective surgery → delay and optimise (e.g. poorly controlled diabetes). Emergency surgery → proceed with whatever optimisation time allows.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is screened in the cardiovascular system pre-operatively, and how useful is functional capacity?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• HTN
  • functional capacity — an important part of risk assessment, though subjective assessment alone predicts post-operative complications poorly
  • red-flag undiagnosed disease (exertional chest pain, syncope, orthopnoea).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is screened in the respiratory system pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Oxygenation and ventilation
  • OSA
  • smoking
  • whether the patient can lie flat and keep still, which is a practical issue for surgery under spinal anaesthesia.
Significant respiratory disease often makes regional anaesthesia preferable to a general anaesthetic — it is not a contraindication to it.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is screened in the renal and endocrine systems pre-operatively, and what else is assessed in older patients?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Renal: baseline function + renal-specific meds
  • Endocrine: especially diabetes and thyroid disease
  • Frailty: score it in every patient aged 65 and over — it predicts adverse post-operative outcome independently of ASA grade, and a frail patient needs comprehensive geriatric assessment and optimisation before surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why does GORD matter pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Aspiration of gastric contents can be fatal → it alters the anaesthetic technique.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What pregnancy and sickle cell considerations apply pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Pregnancy: on the day of surgery, sensitively ask every woman of childbearing potential whether she could be pregnant; do a urinary pregnancy test with her consent if there is any doubt, and document the discussion (NICE)
  • Sickle cell: do not test routinely — ask whether the patient or a family member has sickle cell disease (consider it particularly if born where newborn screening is not routine), and if known and under a specialist service, liaise with that team before surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is covered in the past surgical and anaesthetic history?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Past surgical history — what/when/why; repeat procedures change operative time & difficulty (adhesions)
  • Past anaesthetic history — prior operations, anaesthetic type, any problems.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is covered in the drug, family and social history pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Drug history — full list (some need stopping/changing) + drug & non-drug allergies
  • Family history — general + FHx of anaesthetic problems (especially malignant hyperthermia)
  • Social history — smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs; language/interpreter need; living situation (discharge planning).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What family history is a key anaesthetic red flag?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A family history of anaesthetic problems, especially malignant hyperthermia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the pre-operative examination involve?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• General examination — uncover undiagnosed pathology
  • airway examination — predict difficulty of airway management (intubation)
  • ± operation-relevant area if appropriate.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Which patients are swabbed for MRSA before surgery, and how is a positive result managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Screening is risk-based, not universal: high-risk pathways (orthopaedic, vascular, cardiothoracic, neurosurgery, any prosthetic implant, critical care) and anyone previously MRSA-positive. Swabs from nose + groin/perineum; positive → decolonisation (antiseptic body wash + nasal ointment) before theatre.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When are urinalysis, ECG, and CXR done as routine pre-operative investigations?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Urine testing — dipstick is not routine (NICE); consider MSU microscopy and culture only if a UTI would change the decision to operate
  • ECG — not routine for a fit ASA 1 patient having minor surgery; consider in ASA 2 patients having intermediate surgery with cardiovascular, renal or diabetes comorbidity, and offer for ASA 3–4 and before major or complex surgery
  • CXR — do not routinely offer; order one only if it will change management.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is an FBC and U&Es done pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• FBC: anaemia/thrombocytopenia → correct or prepare blood products; not routine for ASA 1 minor surgery
  • U&Es: baseline kidney function to guide fluids and drug dosing; not routine for ASA 1–2 minor surgery, but consider in anyone at risk of AKI and offer before major or complex surgery (NICE).
Morphine accumulates in renal impairment — reduce the dose and lengthen the interval, avoid modified-release preparations, and use an alternative in severe impairment.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why are LFTs, HbA1c, and TFTs done pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• LFTs: liver metabolism and synthetic function, where liver disease is known or suspected
  • HbA1c: only in people with diagnosed diabetes not tested in the last 3 months — NICE advises against routine HbA1c in people without diabetes
  • TFTs: only if thyroid disease is known or suspected — not a routine pre-operative test.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is a clotting screen done pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Not routinely (NICE). Consider it in chronic liver disease for intermediate or major surgery; an anticoagulated patient needs an individualised plan rather than a screening test.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the difference between a group & save (G&S) and a cross-match?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• G&S: ABO/RhD + atypical antibody screen — if blood might be needed
  • Cross-match: compatibility testing before red cells are issued — if blood will be needed, done after the G&S.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What cardiac investigations are used pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• ECG — offer for ASA 3–4 and before major or complex surgery; consider in ASA 2 patients having intermediate surgery with cardiovascular, renal or diabetes comorbidity (NICE)
  • ECHO — not routine; consider if there is a murmur plus a cardiac symptom (breathlessness, pre-syncope, syncope, chest pain), or signs or symptoms of heart failure, after a resting ECG and discussion with an anaesthetist.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What respiratory/functional capacity investigations are used pre-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Spirometry — pulmonary symptoms or chronic lung disease
  • CPET (cardiopulmonary exercise test) — high-risk patients undergoing major surgery; a graded cycle test giving VO2 max + anaerobic threshold, an objective measure of functional capacity.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is CPET, and what does it measure?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Cardiopulmonary exercise test — for high-risk patients undergoing major surgery; a graded cycle test giving VO2 max + anaerobic threshold, an objective measure of functional capacity.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are ASA grades I and II and their mortality?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• I: a normal healthy patient
  • II: mild systemic disease without substantive functional limitation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are ASA grades III and IV and their mortality?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• III: severe systemic disease with substantive functional limitation, but not a constant threat to life
  • IV: severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is ASA grade V and the meaning of the E suffix?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• V: moribund — not expected to survive without the operation
  • E: a suffix added to any grade for an emergency operation.
(VI describes a brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donation.)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the ASA grade describe, and what is it not?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: It describes physical status, from I (healthy) to V (moribund), with an E suffix for an emergency operation. It broadly tracks operative risk but is not itself a risk-prediction score, and it does not capture frailty.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How useful is exercise tolerance pre-operatively, and how is it quantified objectively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Functional capacity is an important part of risk assessment, but subjective assessment alone predicts complications poorly. CPET quantifies it objectively (VO2 max, anaerobic threshold) in high-risk major surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How should morphine be handled in renal impairment, and when are U&Es needed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Morphine accumulates in renal impairment because of its active metabolite: reduce the dose and lengthen the interval in moderate impairment, avoid modified-release preparations, and use an alternative in severe impairment. Kidney function tests are not routine — consider them in anyone at risk of AKI and before major or complex surgery.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Mallampati score, and what does it predict?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A pre-operative airway assessment graded I–IV by how much of the soft palate/uvula is visible on mouth opening (I = soft palate, uvula and pillars visible; IV = only the hard palate visible). A higher class predicts a more difficult laryngoscopy/intubation — but no single bedside test is reliable alone, so it is combined with thyromental distance, mouth opening, neck mobility and dentition, and a previous difficult intubation is the strongest predictor of all.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does NICE guide routine pre-operative testing for elective surgery?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Tests are not ordered blanket-fashion but are guided by the patient's ASA grade and the severity of surgery (minor / intermediate / major) — e.g. a healthy ASA 1 patient for minor surgery needs few or no routine tests.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the 5 Rs of fluid prescribing (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Resuscitation
  • Routine maintenance
  • Replacement
  • Redistribution (third-spacing, sepsis, liver failure)
  • and Reassessment
Resuscitation, replacement and maintenance are the three you prescribe; redistribution and reassessment shape how you adjust.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is resuscitation fluid indicated, and what is given?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: When the patient is in shock/hypovolaemia. A rapid isotonic bolus to restore perfusion.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is replacement fluid indicated?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: When the patient has ongoing abnormal losses (vomiting, NG, stoma, diarrhoea) — maintenance ± adjustments for deficits and losses.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is maintenance fluid indicated, and what are the daily requirements?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: When the patient is NBM but euvolaemic — just covering daily requirements: 25–30 mL/kg water + 1 mmol/kg Na/K/Cl + 50–100 g glucose.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is total body water distributed between intracellular and extracellular compartments?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Intracellular = ⅔ of total body water. Extracellular = ⅓ — split into intravascular (20%) and interstitial (80%).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the third space, and what is third-spacing?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Third space = peritoneal, pleural, pericardial cavities (don't normally hold fluid). Third-spacing = fluid shifts out of vessels into these spaces → hypovolaemia + oedema simultaneously.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the normal serum osmolality?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 275–295 mOsmol/kg.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an isotonic fluid, where does it stay, and what is it best for?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Isotonic (saline, Hartmann's) → stays extracellular → best for resuscitation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a hypotonic fluid, where does the water go, and what is it used for?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Hypotonic (5% dextrose, 0.18% saline) → water moves into cells → maintenance only; hyponatraemia risk if overused.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a hypertonic fluid and what does it do?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Hypertonic (3% saline) → pulls water out of cells.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the electrolyte composition of 0.9% saline, and what is its use?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Na+ 154, Cl- 154 mmol/L. Use: resuscitation / maintenance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the electrolyte composition of Hartmann's, and its use?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Na+ 131, K+ 5, Cl- 111 mmol/L. Use: resuscitation and replacement as a balanced crystalloid — not routine maintenance, because it delivers far too much sodium and chloride and contains no glucose.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the composition and use of 0.18% NaCl / 4% glucose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Na+ 30, Cl- 30 mmol/L, glucose 40 g/L. Use: maintenance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the composition and use of 5% dextrose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Glucose 50 g/L (no electrolytes). Use: maintenance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 0.9% saline trap, and when is each crystalloid the right choice?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 0.9% saline has Na+ 154 (far above plasma 135–145) and Cl- 154, causing hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis with excess use. For resuscitation and replacement a balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte 148) is the usual default. 0.9% saline is still right where chloride is needed or lactate is unhelpful — hypochloraemic alkalosis from vomiting or NG loss, hyponatraemia, and traumatic brain injury. Neither is a routine maintenance fluid on its own.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are colloids, when are they used, and what is albumin's niche?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Colloids (albumin, Gelofusine) — large molecules, stay intravascular longer. Rarely used (anaphylaxis risk; crystalloids equally effective). Albumin has a niche in decompensated liver disease (↑ oncotic pressure).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the signs of hypovolaemia (↓ECF)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Hypotension (SBP <100), tachycardia (>90)
  • CRT >2 s, cold peripheries
  • ↑RR, dry mucous membranes, ↓skin turgor
  • ↓urine output, sunken eyes, thirst, ↓weight

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the signs of fluid overload (↑ECF)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Peripheral oedema (ankles/sacrum)
  • pulmonary oedema (SOB, ↓sats, ↑RR, bibasal crackles)
  • raised JVP
  • ↑weight from baseline (regular weights = key monitoring tool)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What signs does third-spacing produce, and where is it common?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Signs of BOTH simultaneously: empty intravascular compartment (hypovolaemia signs) + oedematous tissues (overload signs). Common in bowel obstruction, peritonitis, burns.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the NICE fluid resuscitation algorithm?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Fluid: a crystalloid containing sodium 130–154 mmol/L (0.9% saline, Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte 148). Give a 500 mL bolus over less than 15 minutes, reassess ABCDE after every bolus, and repeat 250–500 mL boluses as needed. Seek expert help once more than 2000 mL has been given and the patient is still not responding. In practice use a smaller, slower bolus (e.g. 250 mL) in patients at risk of overload.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does the resuscitation bolus change if there is overload risk?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Give 250 mL (instead of 500 mL) if overload risk (e.g. heart failure).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the potassium safety rule for IV infusion?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Peripherally on a general ward the maximum is 10 mmol/hour, at no more than 40 mmol/L. Faster rates or stronger concentrations need central access, a pump and continuous cardiac monitoring in a critical care setting. Rapid potassium causes arrhythmia and cardiac arrest; never give a rapid bolus with high-potassium bags.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When should you seek senior help during fluid resuscitation?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Get senior help if the patient is shocked or not responding (and after ~2000 mL if not responding). Establish the cause (sepsis, haemorrhage, etc.) alongside resuscitation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the general principles for prescribing maintenance fluids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Use for the shortest time possible and stop as soon as oral intake resumes. Prescribe at the lower end of the range, around 20–25 mL/kg/day, in patients who are older or frail, have renal impairment or cardiac failure, or are malnourished and at risk of refeeding syndrome (NICE). In obese patients calculate on ideal body weight and use the lower volumes per kg — they rarely need more than about 3 L/day. Check U&Es before prescribing potassium, and daily thereafter.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the daily maintenance requirements (water, electrolytes, glucose)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
