• Water: 25–30 mL/kg
  • Na+/K+/Cl-: 1 mmol/kg each
  • Glucose: 50–100 g (anti-ketotic, not nutritional)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the role of glucose in maintenance fluids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Anti-ketotic, not nutritional (50–100 g/day).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the worked maintenance regimen for a 70 kg patient (target ~2 L / 70 mmol Na+K / 50–100 g glucose)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Bag 1: 500 mL 0.9% saline + 20 mmol K+ over 8 h (all Na, ⅓ K, ¼ water)
  • Bag 2: 1 L 5% dextrose + 20 mmol K+ over 8 h (⅓ K, ½ water, glucose)
  • Bag 3: 500 mL 5% dextrose + 20 mmol K+ over 8 h (⅓ K, ¼ water)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the hyponatraemia risk from hypotonic maintenance fluids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: More than 2.5 L/day of hypotonic fluid (0.18% saline + 4% glucose) raises the risk of hyponatraemia (NICE). Do not substitute Hartmann's for routine maintenance — 2 L/day supplies about 262 mmol of sodium against a requirement of roughly 70 mmol, and contains no glucose.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the principle of replacement fluid prescribing?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Replacement = routine maintenance, then add or subtract for existing deficits/excess and ongoing abnormal losses.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is vomiting/NG aspirate high in, and what acid-base consequence results?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High in H+, Cl-, K+. Causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis → replace K+ + Cl-.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is biliary fluid high in, and what is its acid-base consequence?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High in Na+ and HCO3-. Loss of bicarbonate-rich bile causes a metabolic acidosis, as with pancreatic and jejunal losses.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are pancreatic/jejunal losses high in, and what acid-base consequence results?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High in Na+, HCO3-. HCO3- loss → metabolic acidosis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are diarrhoea / new stoma losses high in, and what acid-base consequence results?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: High in Na+, K+, HCO3-. Causes metabolic acidosis + hypokalaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Which IV fluid is preferred in a vomiting patient, and why?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 0.9% saline with added KCl is preferred. Prolonged vomiting/NG loss causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; saline replaces the lost chloride and added potassium corrects the hypokalaemia. Hartmann's is avoided here — its lactate is converted to bicarbonate and would worsen the alkalosis, and its 5 mmol/L K+ is negligible for replacement.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the definition of shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Acute circulatory failure → inadequate tissue oxygen delivery → cellular hypoxia → organ dysfunction. Not simply hypotension.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the DOCH mnemonic for the four types of shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Distributive
  • Obstructive
  • Cardiogenic
  • Hypovolaemic

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and types of distributive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Mechanism: ↓SVR → maldistributed blood flow. Types:
  • septic (most common)
  • anaphylactic
  • neurogenic
  • adrenal

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the haemodynamics, peripheries, and JVP in distributive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Haemodynamics: ↑CO, ↓SVR, ↓BP
  • Peripheries: warm, flushed (early sepsis/anaphylaxis); cold (late)
  • JVP: ↓ (low filling pressure)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and types of obstructive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Mechanism: mechanical obstruction to flow → ↓CO. Types:
  • PE
  • cardiac tamponade
  • tension pneumothorax
  • aortic dissection

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the haemodynamics, peripheries, and JVP in obstructive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Haemodynamics: ↓CO, ↑SVR, ↓BP
  • Peripheries: cold, clammy
  • JVP: ↑↑ (obstructed venous return)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and types of cardiogenic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Mechanism: pump failure → ↓CO. Types:
  • MI (especially anterior STEMI)
  • arrhythmia
  • severe valve disease
  • myocarditis

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the haemodynamics, peripheries, and JVP in cardiogenic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Haemodynamics: ↓CO, ↑SVR, ↓BP
  • Peripheries: cold, clammy
  • JVP: ↑ + pulmonary oedema (wet)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and types of hypovolaemic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Mechanism: ↓preload → ↓CO. Types:
  • haemorrhage (see classes)
  • burns
  • dehydration
  • 3rd spacing

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the haemodynamics, peripheries, and JVP in hypovolaemic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Haemodynamics: ↓CO, ↑SVR, ↓BP
  • Peripheries: cold, clammy
  • JVP: ↓ (reduced filling)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How do the four shock types compare on CO, SVR, JVP, and peripheries?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Distributive: CO ↑, SVR ↓↓, JVP ↓, warm (early)
  • Obstructive: CO ↓, SVR ↑, JVP ↑↑, cold
  • Cardiogenic: CO ↓↓, SVR ↑, JVP ↑, cold + pulmonary oedema
  • Hypovolaemic: CO ↓, SVR ↑, JVP ↓↓, cold

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Which shock type has warm peripheries, and what is the key haemodynamic signature?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Only distributive shock has warm peripheries (early); all others are cold and clammy. Distributive = high CO, low SVR.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the approximate blood volume in adults, and what underlies the ATLS haemorrhage classes?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Blood volume ≈ 70 mL/kg (≈5 L for a 70 kg person). Classes are based on blood loss volume and clinical features.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines ATLS Class I haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Blood loss <750 mL (<15%)
  • HR <100
  • BP normal
  • RR 14–20
  • urine output normal (>30 mL/hr)
  • conscious level normal

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines ATLS Class II haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Blood loss 750–1500 mL (15–30%)
  • HR 100–120
  • BP normal (↑diastolic)
  • RR 20–30
  • urine output 20–30 mL/hr
  • anxious

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines ATLS Class III haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Blood loss 1500–2000 mL (30–40%)
  • HR 120–140
  • BP ↓systolic
  • RR 30–40
  • urine output 5–15 mL/hr
  • confused

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines ATLS Class IV haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Blood loss >2000 mL (>40%)
  • HR >140
  • BP ↓↓systolic
  • RR >40
  • urine output <5 mL/hr
  • lethargic/unconscious

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why is hypotension a late sign in haemorrhage?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: In Class I–II, BP is maintained by compensatory tachycardia + vasoconstriction. BP drops in Class III — by this point ~1.5 L is already lost. Hypotension is a late sign.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is haemorrhagic shock managed (bleeding control, access, fluids)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Stop the bleeding: direct pressure, tourniquet, surgery
  • 2 large-bore IV cannulae (14–16G), bloods including cross-match
  • Crystalloid (Hartmann's): 250–500 mL boluses; reassess after each

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When is the Major Haemorrhage Protocol activated, and what is the blood product ratio?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Class III–IV: activate Major Haemorrhage Protocol → packed RBCs + FFP + platelets (1:1:1).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the volume-resuscitation target in active traumatic bleeding?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: A restrictive approach in any patient with active bleeding until haemorrhage is controlled — titrate to a palpable central pulse (carotid or femoral) rather than a normal blood pressure (NICE); an SBP of around 80–90 mmHg is the commonly taught surrogate. Use a less restrictive approach if traumatic brain injury is the dominant problem, to protect cerebral perfusion.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the role and timing of tranexamic acid in trauma?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g by infusion over 8 hours — as soon as possible and within 3 hours of injury.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the lethal triad of trauma, and how is the cycle broken?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Hypothermia (impairs clotting enzymes; warm ALL fluids, warm patient)
  • acidosis (from tissue hypoxia + lactate; worsens coagulopathy)
  • coagulopathy (dilution from crystalloid, DIC, hypothermia)
Each worsens the others → vicious cycle. Damage control surgery + early blood products break the cycle.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Sepsis-3 definition of sepsis and septic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
  • Septic shock: sepsis + vasopressors needed to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg AND lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the three qSOFA criteria, and what does a score ≥2 mean?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• RR ≥22 breaths/min
  • altered mentation (GCS <15)
  • SBP ≤100 mmHg
Score ≥2 → suspect sepsis and investigate further. It does not replace SOFA, and it is not the UK screening tool — NEWS2 is what UK hospitals use to recognise and escalate sepsis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the SOFA organ dysfunction markers across systems?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Respiratory: PaO₂/FiO₂ <400
  • Renal: creatinine rising, UO <0.5 mL/kg/hr
  • Liver: bilirubin rising
  • Coagulation: platelets falling
  • CNS: GCS falling
  • Cardiovascular: MAP <70 or vasopressors needed

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Sepsis Six, and what sets antibiotic timing in UK practice?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Give 3:
  • oxygen (target SpO₂ 94–98%, or 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic failure)
  • IV antibiotics
  • IV fluids (500 mL–1 L crystalloid bolus if hypotensive or lactate raised)
Take 3:
  • blood cultures (before antibiotics, 2 sets)
  • lactate + bloods
  • urine output (catheterise, target >0.5 mL/kg/hr)
Antibiotic urgency in UK hospitals is set by NEWS2 (NICE): within 1 hour if NEWS2 ≥7, 3 hours if 5–6, 6 hours if 1–4.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Why must antibiotics be given quickly in sepsis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Delay in broad-spectrum IV antibiotics is associated with worse outcomes, most clearly in septic shock. UK timing is stratified by NEWS2 (NICE): within 1 hour if NEWS2 ≥7, 3 hours if 5–6, 6 hours if 1–4, clarifying the diagnosis and targeting therapy in the lower-risk groups.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is done if a septic patient is not responding to initial management?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line, via central line; target MAP ≥65 mmHg) → ICU. Consider hydrocortisone 200 mg/day in refractory septic shock.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and common triggers of anaphylactic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
IgE-mediated (Type I hypersensitivity) → massive mast cell degranulation → histamine, tryptase → ↓SVR + bronchospasm + ↑vascular permeability. Triggers:
  • drugs (penicillin, NSAIDs)
  • foods (nuts)
  • latex
  • stings

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the clinical features of anaphylaxis (skin, airway, breathing, circulation)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Skin: urticaria, erythema, angioedema (lips, tongue, throat)
  • Airway: stridor, hoarseness (laryngeal oedema)
  • Breathing: bronchospasm, wheeze, ↑RR
  • Circulation: tachycardia, ↓BP, warm flushed skin
± nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the FIRST drug and dose in anaphylaxis, and how should the patient be positioned?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Remove the trigger; IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, 1 in 1000) into the anterolateral middle third of the thigh — FIRST, repeated at 5 minutes if no improvement. Lie the patient flat with legs raised (semi-recumbent if breathing is the dominant problem, but still with legs raised); do not sit or stand them up, even if they feel better, because a sudden change of posture can precipitate cardiac arrest.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the adjunctive treatments in anaphylaxis after adrenaline?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• High-flow oxygen
  • call for help
  • IV fluid bolus (500 mL–1 L crystalloid, titrated to response)
Corticosteroids and antihistamines are no longer part of routine emergency management (Resuscitation Council UK) — an antihistamine may be considered after stabilisation for persistent skin symptoms only. If symptoms persist after 2 appropriate IM doses this is refractory anaphylaxis: give further IV fluid and call critical care urgently for an adrenaline infusion. Observation before discharge is risk-stratified from resolution of symptoms (NICE): 2 hours if low risk, 6 hours if 2 doses were needed or there is a history of biphasic reaction, and 12 hours if the reaction was severe, needed more than 2 doses, or there is ongoing allergen absorption or poor access to care. Discharge with
  • two adrenaline auto-injectors
  • device training
  • a written emergency plan and referral to a specialist allergy service

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is serum tryptase used in anaphylaxis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Take ideally three samples:
  • as soon as feasible once treatment has started (never delay resuscitation to take blood)
  • a second 1–2 hours after symptom onset (no later than 4 hours)
  • and a baseline at least 24 hours after the reaction
A rise and fall confirms mast cell activation. Send to immunology.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the commonest cause of cardiogenic shock, and what is the fluid paradox?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Most commonly acute anterior STEMI (LV pump failure); mortality is high. Paradox: giving fluids may worsen pulmonary oedema.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is cardiogenic shock diagnosed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• SBP <90 mmHg AND CO/CI reduced AND adequate filling pressure
  • cold, clammy, ↑JVP, S3 gallop, pulmonary crackles
  • ECG: STEMI, new LBBB
  • Echo: confirms low EF, wall motion abnormality
  • troponin ↑, BNP ↑

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is cardiogenic shock managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Revascularisation ASAP — primary PCI if MI; this is the definitive treatment
  • Vasopressors: noradrenaline (MAP ≥65) ± dobutamine (inotrope)
  • Avoid fluids if pulmonary oedema is present
  • Furosemide if fluid overloaded
Refer early to cardiology and ICU — mechanical circulatory support is a specialist-centre decision.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does tension pneumothorax present and how is it treated immediately?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Distinguishing features:
  • tracheal deviation (away)
  • absent breath sounds
  • raised JVP
  • hyper-resonance
  • hypoxia
It is a clinical diagnosis — do not delay treatment for imaging. Immediate treatment: needle decompression, in adults at the 5th ICS in the anterior/mid-axillary line (the 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line is the traditional alternative), then a chest drain.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does cardiac tamponade present (Beck's triad) and how is it treated immediately?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Beck's triad: ↓BP + ↑JVP + muffled heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg. Echocardiography confirms. Immediate Rx: pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid, ultrasound-guided).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does massive PE present and how is it treated immediately?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Pleuritic pain
  • haemoptysis
  • raised JVP
  • S1Q3T3 on ECG
  • hypoxia
CT-PA confirms. Immediate treatment: systemic thrombolysis (alteplase) if haemodynamically unstable.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the role of fluids in obstructive shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Fluids help temporise (maintain preload) but treat the cause immediately — the obstruction must be relieved. Fluids without relief = futile.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism and unique feature of neurogenic shock?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Spinal cord injury above T6 → loss of sympathetic tone → massive vasodilation. Unique: hypotension + BRADYCARDIA (not tachycardia — unlike all other shocks). Treat with vasopressors (noradrenaline/phenylephrine) + IV fluids + immobilise the spine. Do not confuse it with spinal shock, which is a neurological rather than a circulatory phenomenon — transient flaccid paralysis, sensory loss and areflexia below the injury level, resolving over days to weeks into spasticity and hyperreflexia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the receptor action and use of noradrenaline?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Receptors: α1 >> β1
  • Effect: ↑↑SVR, ↑CO slightly
  • Use: first-line vasopressor in septic, distributive, cardiogenic (with dobutamine)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the receptor action and use of adrenaline?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Receptors: α1, β1, β2
  • Effect: ↑HR, ↑CO, ↑SVR
  • Use: anaphylaxis (IM), cardiac arrest (IV), refractory shock

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the receptor action and use of dobutamine?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Receptors: β1 > β2
  • Effect: ↑CO (inotrope), ↓SVR slightly
  • Use: cardiogenic shock (add to noradrenaline)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the receptor action and use of vasopressin?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Receptor: V1
  • Effect: ↑SVR (vasopressin-deficient in sepsis)
  • Use: add-on in refractory septic shock

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What access do vasopressors need, and what is the usual MAP target?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Vasopressors are ideally given through central venous access, because extravasation from a peripheral line can cause tissue necrosis — but noradrenaline may be started through a dedicated large peripheral cannula as a bridge, so do not delay vasopressor support waiting for a central line. Target MAP ≥65 mmHg in most cases.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a hernia, and what proportion of abdominal hernias are inguinal?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: An organ or its fascia protruding outside the walls of its usual cavity. Inguinal hernias account for 75% of all abdominal hernias.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the two decisive forks when assessing a hernia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Is it complicated? Reducible & wide-necked → safe-ish. Irreducible / narrow-necked → incarceration → obstruction and/or strangulation. The stages usually run in that order but not always — in a Richter's hernia only part of the bowel circumference is trapped, so the lumen stays open and it can strangulate and perforate without ever obstructing.
  • Which anatomical type? Each is defined by where it emerges.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the typical presentation of a hernia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Soft lump through the abdominal wall
  • reducible — pushes back on lying down or gentle pressure
  • protrudes on coughing (↑ intra-abdominal pressure) or standing (gravity)
  • aching/dragging sensation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the structured check when examining a groin lump?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Cough impulse (an irreducible hernia may lose this)
  • location relative to the pubic tubercle (the key discriminator)
  • reducible on lying down / gentle pressure?
  • if entering scrotum — can you get above it / separate it from the testis?

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the single highest-yield discriminator between inguinal and femoral hernias?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Inguinal = superomedial to the pubic tubercle.
  • Femoral = inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does neck width drive the risk of a hernia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Wide neck = reduces easily, lower risk.
  • Narrow neck = high risk — the bowel gets trapped and cannot decompress.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is incarceration in the hernia deterioration ladder?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Irreducible — bowel trapped in the sac, cannot be reduced. Presents as a firm, tender lump that won't reduce; a precursor to obstruction and/or strangulation (a Richter's hernia can strangulate without ever obstructing).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the obstruction stage in the hernia deterioration ladder?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Trapped bowel blocks faecal flow. Presents as
  • vomiting
  • generalised pain
  • and absolute constipation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is strangulation in the hernia deterioration ladder?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The neck cuts off the blood supply → ischaemia → infarction. Red flags: an irreducible, tender hernia with overlying skin changes, tachycardia, fever or peritonism — a surgical emergency (infarcts within hours). Do not attempt to reduce it.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the three management options for a hernia, and which repair does UK practice use?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Conservative (watchful waiting) — the default for an asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia in a man; repair is offered if it becomes symptomatic, irreducible, or limits normal work or activity. Not an option for femoral hernias.
  • Tension-free mesh repair (preferred) — open mesh repair is standard for a primary unilateral inguinal hernia, and laparoscopic repair is preferred for bilateral and recurrent hernias (NICE).
  • Tension repair — sutures pull the defect edges together; rarely used (painful, high recurrence).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the emergency management of a strangulated hernia, and what is the rule for all femoral hernias?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Do not attempt to reduce a hernia that is irreducible and tender, or has overlying skin changes or systemic upset — forcing ischaemic bowel back into the abdomen risks perforation.
  • Resuscitate (IV access, fluids, analgesia, nil by mouth, IV antibiotics if septic) and go to theatre; resect ischaemic/necrotic bowel.
  • All femoral hernias are repaired surgically and urgently, because the narrow rigid ring gives a high strangulation risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What proportion of abdominal wall hernias are inguinal, what proportion of inguinal hernias are indirect, and which sex predominates?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Inguinal hernias are 75% of abdominal wall hernias.
  • Indirect 80%, direct 20%.
  • The great majority occur in men.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Compare the mechanism of indirect vs direct inguinal hernias.
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Indirect: bowel through the inguinal canal (patent processus vaginalis).
  • Direct: weakness at Hesselbach's triangle.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How do indirect vs direct inguinal hernias relate to the inferior epigastric vessels?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Indirect: lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
  • Direct: medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Can direct and indirect inguinal hernias be told apart on clinical examination?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: No. The deep-ring (occlusion) test is unreliable and the type is confirmed at operation. It does not change management — both are repaired with tension-free mesh. The distinction that matters clinically is inguinal versus femoral, made by position relative to the pubic tubercle.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Compare the origin of indirect vs direct inguinal hernias.
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Indirect: congenital (failure of the processus vaginalis to obliterate).
  • Direct: acquired wall weakness.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the borders of Hesselbach's triangle (R-I-P)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Rectus abdominis (medial border)
  • inferior epigastric vessels (lateral border)
  • Poupart's / inguinal ligament (inferior border).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What does the inguinal canal carry, and what is the deep-ring landmark?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• The canal runs deep ring → superficial ring; it carries the spermatic cord (male) / round ligament (female).
  • Deep ring landmark: midpoint of ASIS → pubic tubercle.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the differential for a groin or scrotal lump, and how do you separate a hernia from a hydrocele?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Femoral hernia
  • hydrocele
  • lymph node
  • saphena varix
  • femoral aneurysm
  • undescended testis.
You can get above a hydrocele but not above an inguinal hernia; transillumination supports a hydrocele but is unreliable in neonates, where both may transilluminate.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Where does a femoral hernia emerge, who is it commoner in, and why are all repaired?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Through the femoral canal, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.
  • Commoner in women (especially multiparous) — but inguinal hernia is still the commonest hernia in women overall.
  • The femoral ring has narrow, rigid borders → high strangulation risk → all femoral hernias are repaired surgically, and urgently.
Because inguinal and femoral hernias cannot be told apart reliably at the bedside, refer any groin hernia in a woman urgently.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the borders of the femoral canal (F-L-I-P)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Femoral vein (lateral)
  • lacunar ligament (medial)
  • inguinal ligament (anterior)
  • pectineal ligament (posterior).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines an incisional and an umbilical hernia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Incisional: at a previous surgical scar. Risk factors include wound infection, emergency surgery, a midline incision, obesity, smoking, diabetes and steroids. Repaired if symptomatic; conservative if asymptomatic or a poor surgical candidate; recurrence after repair is high.
  • Umbilical: symmetrical bulge through the umbilicus. In children it usually closes spontaneously, most by age 3, and is unlikely to close after about 4 — refer if it persists beyond 4–5 years, is very large, or complicates. Also occurs in adults.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines a paraumbilical and an epigastric hernia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Paraumbilical: asymmetrical bulge just above/below the umbilicus (not through it). Adults; a narrow fibrous neck means it does not resolve and carries a real strangulation risk, so it is usually repaired.
  • Epigastric: through linea alba fibres; differential = divarication of recti (no true hernia).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What defines a parastomal and a Spigelian hernia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Parastomal: through a stoma site.
  • Spigelian: rare; at the semilunar line (lateral rectus border, ~arcuate line); a small tender mass with high strangulation risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an obturator hernia, who gets it, and what is the classic sign?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Through the obturator foramen; elderly, thin, multiparous women + rapid weight loss (the foramen is normally fat-filled).
  • There is no visible lump — it typically presents as unexplained small bowel obstruction in a thin elderly woman, and CT makes the diagnosis.
  • Howship–Romberg sign: medial thigh/knee pain on internal rotation of the hip = obturator nerve compression; helpful when present but often absent.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a hiatus hernia, and what does it disrupt?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• The stomach herniates through the diaphragm into the thorax.
  • Widening of the normally narrow, fixed hiatus disrupts the LOS → reflux.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a type 1 (sliding) hiatus hernia, and what does it cause?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The commonest type. The GOJ slides up into the thorax; the GOJ and fundus move together → causes GORD.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a type 2 (rolling / paraoesophageal) hiatus hernia, and why is it significant?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: The fundus rolls up alongside the oesophagus; the GOJ stays put. It carries a higher strangulation risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are type 3 and type 4 hiatus hernias?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Type 3: combination sliding + rolling — both the GOJ and fundus herniate.
  • Type 4: a large defect — other organs (bowel, pancreas, omentum) enter the thorax.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the risk factors, symptoms, and investigations for a hiatus hernia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Risk factors: age, obesity, pregnancy.
  • Dyspepsia symptoms: heartburn, acid/food reflux, burping, bloating, halitosis.
  • Seen on CXR, CT, endoscopy, barium swallow.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a hiatus hernia managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Conservative — treat GORD medically (PPI, lifestyle).
  • Laparoscopic fundoplication — wrap the fundus around the lower oesophagus to tighten the LOS; if high-risk or refractory.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the examined skill in post-operative complications, and what are the two organising axes?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Early recognition — haemorrhage and sepsis especially, as patients can deteriorate within hours. Two organising axes: by system (respiratory, cardiovascular, GI, urinary, wound, haematological) and by timing (immediate → early → late). The post-operative pyrexia timeline is the highest-yield application.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the principle behind the post-operative pyrexia 5 Ws?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
The timing of fever narrows the differential before you examine the patient:
  • early fever = respiratory
  • later fever = wound / VTE / collection.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 'Wind' W (day 0–2) — cause and key action?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Cause: atelectasis, pneumonia
  • Key action: analgesia, chest physio, mobilise, deep breathing.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 'Water' W (day 3–5) — cause and key action?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Cause: UTI (catheter-associated)
  • Key action: urine dip/MSU, remove catheter early.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 'Walking' W (day 4–6) — cause and key action?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Cause: DVT / PE
  • Key action: Doppler USS leg, CTPA; LMWH; TEDs.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 'Wound' W (day 5–7) — cause and key action?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Cause: SSI, anastomotic leak
  • Key action: inspect wound, examine abdomen, bloods + CT.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the 'Wonder drugs / What's in the line' W (any time) — cause and key action?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Cause: drug reaction, transfusion reaction, line/cannula sepsis
  • Key action: review drug chart, change/remove lines, blood cultures.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does post-operative haemorrhage present, and when is it recognised late?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Bleeding into a drain, internally as a haematoma, or from the wound → untreated leads to hypovolaemic shock (tachycardia, ↓BP, pale/clammy). Recognise fast — BP is maintained until Class III (>1.5 L lost).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the three types of post-operative haemorrhage by timing and mechanism?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Primary (intra-operative): bleeding during surgery from a vessel
  • Reactive (within 24 h): slipped ligature or missed vessel as BP normalises post-op
  • Secondary (7–10 days): infection erodes a vessel — often sudden haemorrhage into a previously healing wound.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is post-operative haemorrhage managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Resuscitate (large-bore IV ×2, bloods, cross-match, IV fluids/blood), identify the bleeding source, urgent surgical review. Secondary haemorrhage = infection control + surgical re-exploration.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is atelectasis, when does it occur, and does it cause fever?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Collapse of lung segments due to under-ventilation (pain → shallow breathing → mucous plugging), commonest on day 0–2. Presents with a raised RR, falling SpO₂ and reduced air entry at the bases; CXR shows basal shadowing. It does not itself cause fever — the classic teaching is not supported by the evidence, so if the patient is febrile look for another cause. Management: adequate analgesia (allows deep breathing), chest physiotherapy, mobilisation, incentive spirometry.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does post-operative pneumonia present, and what increases the risk?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Hospital-acquired (HAP) — gram-negative organisms common.
  • Presents: fever, productive cough, ↑WCC, consolidation on CXR
  • Management: sputum culture, antibiotics per local protocol, O₂, physio
  • Risk ↑ with: prolonged ventilation, aspiration (dysphagia, NGT), immunosuppression.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the analgesia link in respiratory complications?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Adequate pain relief allows deep breathing and mobilisation → reduces atelectasis → reduces pneumonia. Under-treated pain → shallow breathing → retained secretions → infection.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How do post-operative DVT and PE present (day 4–6)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• DVT: unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, erythema
  • PE: pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, ↑HR, hypoxia; massive PE → haemodynamic collapse.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the investigations, prevention, and treatment of post-operative VTE?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Investigations: go straight to imaging — Doppler USS (DVT), CTPA (PE). D-dimer is unhelpful post-operatively because surgery itself raises it
  • Prevention: LMWH + anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression + early mobilisation, extended to 28 days after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery
  • Treatment: apixaban or rivaroxaban first-line (NICE); therapeutic LMWH where a DOAC is unsuitable or reversibility matters immediately post-op.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What cardiac complications occur post-operatively (arrhythmias, ACS/MI, stroke)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Arrhythmias — especially new AF (surgery triggers sympathetic activation, hypoxia and electrolyte disturbance); after bowel surgery, new AF is an anastomotic leak until proven otherwise
  • ACS/MI — surgical stress unmasks coronary disease; most occur in the first 48 hours, and the majority are silent because analgesia masks the pain, presenting instead as unexplained hypotension, tachycardia, new AF, breathlessness or confusion
  • Stroke — embolic (AF, air embolus) or haemorrhagic.
Risk is higher with pre-existing cardiac disease, major vascular surgery and emergency operations.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is post-operative ileus, and how does it present?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Functional bowel dysmotility — not mechanical obstruction. Common after abdominal or pelvic surgery, long anaesthetics, opioids and electrolyte disturbance. Presents with abdominal distension, vomiting, a silent abdomen with absent bowel sounds, and no flatus or stool. AXR shows dilated loops throughout. Management: IV fluids, correct electrolytes especially K+, mobilise, minimise opioids; an NG tube is for symptomatic relief of significant distension and vomiting with aspiration risk, not to hasten resolution.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does an anastomotic leak present, and how is it managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Breakdown of a bowel join → GI contents into the peritoneum, classically day 5–7 but anywhere from day 2 to day 14. The late picture is increasing pain, fever, peritonism and sepsis with faeculent or turbid drain output and a sharply rising CRP on day 3–5. The exam trap is the earlier picture: a patient who looks well but has unexplained persistent tachycardia, new-onset AF, oliguria, prolonged ileus or simple failure to progress. CT abdomen with contrast confirms it. Management: resuscitate, IV antibiotics, urgent senior surgical review; a small contained leak in a stable patient may be drained radiologically, while peritonitis, sepsis or a large leak needs urgent re-operation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is post-operative ileus distinguished from mechanical obstruction?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Ileus: dilated loops throughout on AXR, with a silent abdomen and absent bowel sounds
  • Obstruction: dilated proximal and decompressed distal bowel, with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds and colicky pain.
AXR is suggestive only — CT with contrast is what actually distinguishes them if the ileus is not settling by day 3–4.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the late GI complications post-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Adhesions → small bowel obstruction (the most common cause of SBO in adults)
  • Incisional hernia → protrusion through the scar (especially midline laparotomy); risk ↑ with obesity, infection, poor nutrition, steroids
  • Constipation — opioids + immobility; prescribe laxatives with opioids routinely.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does a surgical site infection present, when, and how is it classified by depth?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Erythema, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge and wound pain, with or without systemic sepsis — most often day 5–10, and by definition within 30 days of surgery (longer where an implant is used).
  • Superficial: skin and subcutaneous tissue
  • deep: fascia and muscle
  • organ/space (e.g. intra-abdominal abscess).
Organisms: Staphylococcus aureus is commonest overall; after bowel surgery expect Gram-negatives and anaerobes. A wound infection in the first 24–48 hours with pain out of proportion, crepitus or rapidly spreading erythema suggests a necrotising infection — a surgical emergency.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is a surgical site infection managed and prevented?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Management: wound swab, open and drain superficial infections, antibiotics for systemic features
  • Prevention: chlorhexidine skin prep, prophylactic antibiotics at induction, normothermia, normoglycaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the difference between wound dehiscence and burst abdomen?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Dehiscence: partial separation of wound edges
  • Burst abdomen (evisceration): full-thickness separation with bowel/omentum protruding through skin — a surgical emergency.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the warning sign of burst abdomen, and how is it managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Warning sign: serosanguineous "pink fluid" draining from the wound (day 5–10). Management:
  • cover the wound and any protruding bowel with saline-soaked sterile gauze
  • nil by mouth, IV access, IV fluid resuscitation, adequate analgesia, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and an NG tube
  • urgent senior surgical review and return to theatre for washout and mass closure with non-absorbable sutures.
Risk is higher with obesity, malnutrition, infection, steroids, poor surgical technique and coughing.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does a post-operative UTI present (day 3–5), and how is it managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Catheter-associated UTI is a common healthcare-associated infection post-op, and the great majority are catheter-related. Dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, cloudy urine, with or without systemic sepsis.
  • Investigations: urine dip, MSU + culture
  • Management: antibiotics per local protocol, and remove the catheter as soon as possible.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How does post-operative urinary retention present and get managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Presents as inability to pass urine with suprapubic discomfort and a palpable or percussible bladder; in a confused or post-operative patient it may present only as agitation or delirium, or as overflow dribbling. Common causes: opioids, spinal anaesthesia, pelvic surgery, pain, constipation, anticholinergics; commoner in men (BPH). Management: confirm with a bedside bladder scan before catheterising — this avoids unnecessary catheters and the CAUTIs they cause — then catheterise, treat the precipitants, and arrange a trial without catheter (TWOC).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What causes post-operative AKI, and how is it managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Hypovolaemia, sepsis and nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, gentamicin, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, contrast) → oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) → rising creatinine. Management: identify and treat the cause — stop or withhold nephrotoxics and review the whole drug chart, exclude obstruction (bladder scan; flush or replace a blocked catheter), treat sepsis, and give a fluid challenge if hypovolaemic. Monitor urine output and U&Es, and check for hyperkalaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the causes and transfusion thresholds for post-operative anaemia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Post-op FBC at 24–48 h; causes: intra-operative blood loss, haemodilution, haemolysis. Investigate the cause and treat iron-deficiency anaemia with oral or IV iron (NICE) rather than transfusing.
  • Transfuse at Hb <70 g/L with a target of 70–90 g/L
  • <80 g/L with a target of 80–100 g/L in acute coronary syndrome.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How are Jehovah's Witnesses managed regarding transfusion?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: They may refuse transfusion by a valid advance directive — respect autonomy if capacity is present; optimise pre-op, use cell salvage, minimise intra-op loss.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the Apfel score for PONV, and what is the prophylaxis?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Risk factors (Apfel score): female, non-smoker, prior PONV or motion sickness, post-operative opioids (each = 1 point; score 3 or more = high risk)
  • Prophylaxis: ondansetron + dexamethasone at induction (± cyclizine) in high-risk patients; use TIVA (propofol) instead of volatile agents
  • Treatment: ondansetron 4 mg IV/IM, or cyclizine 50 mg IV.
Metoclopramide 10 mg IV is an option but is a prokinetic — avoid it in the first 3–4 days after bowel surgery with an anastomosis, and in obstruction or perforation; it is restricted to short-term use (maximum 5 days) because of extrapyramidal side effects (MHRA).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the reversible causes of post-operative delirium (PINCH ME)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Pain
  • Infection
  • Nutrition
  • Constipation
  • Hydration
  • Medication
  • Environment.
Acute fluctuating confusion — common in elderly/frail post-op. Exclude: hypoxia, sepsis, urinary retention, hypoglycaemia.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: How is post-operative delirium managed?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Screen with the 4AT — delirium is under-recognised, particularly the hypoactive form. Identify and treat the cause (PINCH ME; exclude hypoxia, sepsis, urinary retention, hypoglycaemia).
  • Non-pharmacological measures first: reorientation, familiar staff and faces, glasses and hearing aids, daylight and sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, treat pain and constipation
  • Only if the patient is distressed or a risk to themselves or others and de-escalation has failed, consider short-term (usually up to a week) haloperidol at the lowest effective dose (NICE) — avoid in Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia
  • Avoid benzodiazepines, which worsen delirium; the exception is alcohol withdrawal, where they are the treatment.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the principles of post-operative nutrition?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Enteral preferred (oral → NG/PEG → jejunostomy)
  • Early feeding (day of surgery in ERAS) reduces infective complications + ileus + LOS
  • TPN via central line only if the GI tract is completely unusable — hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins
  • Screen with MUST; dietitian if complex needs.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the multimodal analgesic ladder post-operatively?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Step 1: regular paracetamol 1 g QDS
  • Step 2: add an NSAID (ibuprofen or naproxen) — avoid in renal impairment, peptic ulcer disease, established cardiovascular disease and heart failure, and in anyone with previous NSAID or aspirin hypersensitivity (ask about this specifically in asthmatics); systemic diclofenac is contraindicated in established ischaemic heart, peripheral arterial or cerebrovascular disease and moderate-to-severe heart failure (MHRA)
  • Step 3: add a weak opioid (codeine, tramadol) or strong opioid (morphine, oxycodone).
Prescribe laxatives with all opioids to prevent opioid-induced constipation. Regional techniques (epidural, nerve block) reduce systemic opioid requirements — and reducing opioid load is what reduces ileus.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is patient-controlled analgesia (PCA), and what is its key safety mechanism?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
IV opioid on-demand with a lockout interval. Only the patient presses the button — a safety mechanism; staff/family must not press it. Have available:
  • naloxone (respiratory depression)
  • antiemetic (PONV)
  • atropine (bradycardia).
Review daily — wean when oral intake is re-established.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: When should each line, tube and drain be removed (ERAS principle)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Urinary catheter: remove when mobile and there is no urological indication → TWOC; retention risk in males
  • Drains: remove when output is under 30 mL/24 h (or per surgeon — timing is contested)
  • IV cannula: inspect daily for phlebitis and re-site when clinically indicated — routine replacement at a fixed interval is no longer recommended
  • NGT: remove when GI function returns and oral intake is adequate.
Every device left in longer than needed increases infection risk and impairs mobilisation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: WHO analgesic ladder: Step 1?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Non-opioid: paracetamol + NSAIDs (regular, not PRN)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: WHO analgesic ladder: Step 2?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Add weak opioid: codeine, tramadol, dihydrocodeine

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: WHO analgesic ladder: Step 3?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Strong opioid: morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, buprenorphine

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What should always be co-prescribed with opioids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Laxatives (e.g. senna + lactulose) — prevent constipation

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Which opioid is preferred in renal failure?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Fentanyl (avoids accumulation of active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide)

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: NSAIDs contraindications?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• CKD
  • peptic ulcer disease
  • HF
  • asthma (aspirin-sensitive)
  • 3rd trimester pregnancy

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Antidote for opioid overdose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Naloxone (opioid antagonist) — reverses analgesia too

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Maximum dose of plain lidocaine?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 3 mg/kg

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Maximum dose of lidocaine with adrenaline?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 7 mg/kg

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Maximum dose of bupivacaine?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: 2 mg/kg

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Signs of local anaesthetic toxicity?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Perioral tingling → tinnitus → seizures → cardiovascular collapse

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: Treatment for LA toxicity?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Intralipid 20% (lipid emulsion) IV + resuscitation

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the WHO analgesic ladder?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Step 1: Non-opioids (paracetamol, NSAIDs)
  • Step 2: Mild opioids ± non-opioids (codeine, tramadol)
  • Step 3: Strong opioids ± non-opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl).
Adjuvants at each step.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the adjuvant analgesics?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline — neuropathic pain)
  • gabapentinoids (gabapentin/pregabalin — neuropathic)
  • corticosteroids (nerve/tumour compression)
  • ketamine
  • clonidine
  • capsaicin.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism of action of paracetamol?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Inhibits prostaglandin synthesis centrally (COX-3 in CNS); also activates endocannabinoid system and serotonergic descending pathways. Does NOT inhibit peripheral COX (no anti-inflammatory effect).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is paracetamol toxicity and its mechanism?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Overdose → NAPQI accumulation (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) when glutathione stores depleted → hepatocellular necrosis. Treatment: N-acetylcysteine (glutathione precursor), liver transplant if fulminant failure.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism of NSAIDs?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Inhibit COX-1 and COX-2 → ↓prostaglandins (PGE₂, PGI₂) → analgesia, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic effect.
  • COX-1 inhibition → GI toxicity, platelet inhibition
  • COX-2 inhibition → analgesic/anti-inflammatory, CV risk.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the contraindications to NSAIDs?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Peptic ulcer disease
  • CKD (reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal perfusion)
  • heart failure (fluid retention)
  • asthma (aspirin-induced asthma)
  • pregnancy (premature ductus arteriosus closure)
  • anticoagulation (bleeding risk).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the mechanism of opioids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Bind μ (mu), κ (kappa), δ (delta) opioid receptors → inhibit adenylate cyclase → ↓cAMP → ↓neurotransmitter release → reduced pain transmission in dorsal horn and supraspinal centres.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the side effects of opioids?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Constipation (μ receptors in gut)
  • nausea/vomiting
  • sedation
  • respiratory depression
  • pruritus
  • urinary retention
  • tolerance
  • dependence
  • myosis (pinpoint pupils — diagnostic of opioid overdose).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What reverses opioid overdose?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Naloxone (opioid receptor antagonist) — IV/IM/intranasal; short half-life (30–90 min) so repeated doses or infusion needed for long-acting opioids; reverses respiratory depression, sedation, and miosis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the difference between opioid tolerance and dependence?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Tolerance = reduced effect with repeated dosing (requires higher dose)
  • Dependence = physiological withdrawal on cessation.
Addiction = compulsive drug-seeking behaviour despite harm (psychological component).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What opioids are used in step 2 vs step 3 of the pain ladder?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Step 2: codeine, tramadol, dihydrocodeine (weak opioids)
  • Step 3: morphine (gold standard), oxycodone, fentanyl (transdermal patch), buprenorphine, methadone, diamorphine (subcutaneous in syringe driver).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the conversion between oral morphine and SC diamorphine?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Oral morphine : SC diamorphine = 3:1 (oral morphine 30 mg/day = SC diamorphine 10 mg/day). Used in palliative care syringe drivers.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What are the types of pain (classification)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Nociceptive (somatic — sharp, localised; visceral — dull, diffuse, referred)
  • neuropathic (burning, shooting, allodynia — nerve damage)
  • inflammatory
  • cancer pain (mixed).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is neuropathic pain and how is it treated?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Pain from nerve injury/dysfunction — burning, shooting, allodynia (pain from non-painful stimulus), hyperalgesia. Treated with:
  • amitriptyline (first-line)
  • duloxetine
  • gabapentin/pregabalin
  • topical capsaicin
  • SNRIs.
Opioids have limited effect.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the difference between allodynia and hyperalgesia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Allodynia = pain from a normally non-painful stimulus (e.g., light touch)
  • Hyperalgesia = increased pain from a normally painful stimulus.
Both are features of central and peripheral sensitisation.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a syringe driver and when is it used?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Continuous subcutaneous infusion device — used in palliative care when patient cannot take oral medications (vomiting, dysphagia, unconscious). Combines diamorphine (pain), midazolam (agitation), haloperidol (nausea), and hyoscine (secretions).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the ABCDE mnemonic for acute pain management?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Not a standard mnemonic for pain — rather:
  • assess severity (NRS/VAS)
  • choose appropriate ladder step
  • consider route (IV/IM/oral/SC)
  • evaluate regularly
  • and adjust.
Multimodal analgesia reduces opioid requirements.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is multimodal analgesia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Combination of analgesics from different classes targeting different pain pathways — e.g., paracetamol + NSAID + opioid + nerve block = opioid-sparing effect, better pain control, fewer side effects. Basis of ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is an epidural and what is it used for?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Local anaesthetic ± opioid infusion into the epidural space (L3/L4 or T10) — provides excellent analgesia for thoracic/abdominal/lower limb surgery. Complications: hypotension, urinary retention, epidural haematoma/abscess (rare).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is a nerve block and give examples?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
Regional anaesthetic technique — infiltrating local anaesthetic around specific nerves. Examples:
  • femoral nerve block (hip/femur surgery)
  • brachial plexus block (upper limb)
  • intercostal block (rib/thoracic)
  • TAP block (abdominal wall — transversus abdominis plane).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is tramadol's mechanism of action?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Dual mechanism: weak μ-opioid agonist + inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake (SNRI-like). Risk of serotonin syndrome (especially with SSRIs, MAOIs). Lowers seizure threshold. Step 2 opioid.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the risk of tramadol with SSRIs?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Serotonin syndrome — excessive serotonergic activity → hyperthermia, confusion, agitation, clonus, diaphoresis, tachycardia. Can be fatal. Tramadol + SSRIs/MAOIs/TCAs is a significant drug interaction.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the role of gabapentin and pregabalin in pain management?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Gabapentinoids — bind α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels → reduce neuronal excitability and pain signal transmission. A first-line option for neuropathic pain (diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia). Perioperative adjuncts.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is breakthrough analgesia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Additional 'rescue' doses of opioid given for sudden pain despite background analgesia — typically 1/6 of the 24-hour total opioid dose, given 4-hourly as needed. Important in palliative care.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: IV opioid pump (morphine/fentanyl) allowing patient-controlled demand doses within set lockout intervals — provides individualised pain control, improves satisfaction, and reduces nurse workload. Used post-operatively.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is the analgesic ceiling effect?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back: Some analgesics (e.g., codeine, aspirin) have a maximum dose beyond which no additional analgesia is gained but side effects increase. Strong opioids (morphine) do NOT have a ceiling effect — dose is limited only by side effects.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: What is ketamine and when is it used in analgesia?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
NMDA receptor antagonist — dissociative anaesthetic at high doses; analgesic at sub-anaesthetic doses. Used for:
  • procedural pain
  • neuropathic pain
  • opioid-refractory pain
  • burn dressing changes.
Causes hallucinations/dysphoria (use with midazolam).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the three steps of the WHO analgesic ladder?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.back:
• Step 1 = non-opioids (paracetamol, NSAIDs)
  • Step 2 = weak opioids (codeine, tramadol)
  • Step 3 = strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone).
Adjuvants at each step. Principle: by the clock, by the mouth, by the ladder.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the decisive principle governing every nutritional route decision?
options: Choose the least invasive route the gut can tolerate
Use a PEG in every malnourished patient
Choose the most invasive route available
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Choose the least invasive route the gut can tolerate
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The decisive fork is to choose the least invasive route the gut can tolerate — 'if the gut works, use it' — progressing oral → enteral → parenteral.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: When is enteral (tube) feeding appropriate?
options: Any patient who can swallow safely
Unsafe or inadequate oral intake with a functional gut
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Unsafe or inadequate oral intake with a functional gut
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Enteral tube feeding is used when oral intake is unsafe/inadequate but the GI tract is functional and accessible; both conditions must hold.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: When is parenteral (IV) nutrition indicated?
options: When the patient can still swallow safely
As first-line for all post-operative patients
When oral supplements are declined by the patient
Whenever a patient is found to be malnourished
When the gut is non-functional or inaccessible
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: When the gut is non-functional or inaccessible
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Parenteral nutrition is for when the GI tract is non-functional, inaccessible or perforated — it does not require a working gut.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which screening tool and schedule does NICE recommend for inpatients?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: MUST on admission, repeated weekly
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: All inpatients are screened with MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool) on admission and weekly thereafter; outpatients are screened at first appointment.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which criterion defines a patient as malnourished?
options: Any weight loss over the past year
A BMI below 25 on its own
Poor absorptive capacity on its own
Having eaten little for more than 5 days only
BMI <18.5, or >10% loss, or BMI <20 with >5% loss
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: BMI <18.5, or >10% loss, or BMI <20 with >5% loss
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: A patient is malnourished if any one applies: BMI <18.5; unintentional weight loss >10% in 3–6 months; or BMI <20 plus weight loss >5% in 3–6 months.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which of the following meets the NICE criteria for being 'at risk of malnutrition', as distinct from already being malnourished?
options: A BMI below 20 with over 5% weight loss
Little or no intake >5 days, or poor absorption
A BMI below 18.5 on its own
Unintentional weight loss over 10% in 3–6 months
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Little or no intake >5 days, or poor absorption
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: NICE separates patients who are already malnourished (defined by BMI and weight-loss criteria) from those 'at risk of malnutrition', which is defined by intake and absorption: having eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days (or likely to for the next 5 or more), poor absorptive capacity or high nutrient losses, or increased needs from catabolism.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the daily energy target for a patient who is not severely ill and has no refeeding risk?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: 25–35 kcal/kg (lower if BMI >25)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Daily targets (not severely ill, no refeeding risk) are energy 25–35 kcal/kg (lower if BMI >25), protein 0.8–1.5 g/kg and fluid 30–35 mL/kg.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How are feeding targets adjusted for someone who has eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days?
options: Start at ≤50% of requirements for the first 2 days
Use parenteral nutrition instead of enteral
Start at the full target immediately
Withhold all feeding for a further 7 days
Give double the target to catch up quickly
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Start at ≤50% of requirements for the first 2 days
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: For someone who has eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days, start nutrition support at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days, then increase if monitoring shows no refeeding problems. In severe illness or injury, start at no more than 50% of target and build up over 24–48 hours as tolerated.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient needs tube feeding for an expected 2 weeks with a normal stomach and no reflux. Which route is most appropriate?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Nasogastric (NG)
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: For short-term feeding (<4 weeks) with a normal stomach, an NG tube is used — it is the most common, allows bolus and hypertonic feeds, but is easily displaced.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which feeding route reduces aspiration risk in a patient with delayed gastric emptying or reflux?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Nasojejunal (NJ) — post-pyloric
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: An NJ tube (jejunum, nasal) reduces aspiration risk and is used for delayed gastric emptying/reflux, though post-pyloric placement can be difficult.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A stroke patient is expected to need tube feeding for several months. Which route is most appropriate, and when is it usable?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: PEG; usable 4 hours after insertion
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: For long-term feeding (≥4 weeks) in conditions like stroke, MND, Parkinson's or oesophageal cancer, a PEG is placed endoscopically under antibiotic cover and is usable 4 hours after insertion.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the '4-week rule' for feeding routes?
options: Always use NG regardless of duration
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: <4 weeks → NG; ≥4 weeks → consider PEG
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The 4-week rule: feeding needed for less than 4 weeks → NG; 4 weeks or more → consider a gastrostomy (PEG).

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How is NG tube position confirmed before every use (NHS England)?
options: Aspirate a pH of 7 or above on pH paper
Check position only once after insertion
Aspirate pH 1–5.5 on CE-marked pH paper
Confirm by watching the feed flow freely
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Aspirate pH 1–5.5 on CE-marked pH paper
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: NG position is confirmed after placement, before every use, and after vomiting, retching or coughing, by aspirating pH 1–5.5 on CE-marked pH indicator paper. If the pH is above 5.5 or no aspirate can be obtained, do not feed — get a chest X-ray reported by a competent trained assessor. Auscultation (the "whoosh" test) is unreliable and must never be used, and giving a feed through an undetected misplaced tube is a Never Event.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A feed is given through an NG tube misplaced in the respiratory tract, the misplacement having gone undetected. How is this classified?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: A Never Event
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Undetected misplacement — a feed, flush or medication given through a tube in the pleura or respiratory tract — is a Never Event. Misplacement detected at the placement check and never used is not: it is a recognised occurrence at insertion, which is why the pH check before every use is mandatory.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Why is TPN typically given via a central line rather than a peripheral vein?
options: The hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins
It avoids the need for monitoring
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: The hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: TPN is typically given via a central line because the hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins; the line type depends on the expected duration.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which PN access is appropriate for feeding expected to last more than 30 days?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Tunnelled subclavian line
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: For >30 days (long-term) PN, a tunnelled subclavian line is used; <14 days with no other central need can use a peripheral venous catheter, and <30 days a non-tunnelled central catheter.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the most significant complication of parenteral nutrition?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Line sepsis
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Line sepsis is the big PN complication, requiring daily catheter-site inspection; others include thrombosis, refeeding syndrome, deranged LFTs/cholestasis and electrolyte/glucose disturbance.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the purpose of trophic feeding alongside parenteral nutrition?
options: It provides all of the patient's calorie needs
Minimal enteral feed maintains gut function
It treats an established line sepsis
It removes the need for a central venous line
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Minimal enteral feed maintains gut function
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Trophic feeding keeps minimal enteral feeding alongside PN where possible, maintaining gut function and reducing cholestasis.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What is the underlying mechanism of refeeding syndrome?
options: Insulin surge shifting phosphate, K+ and Mg2+ into cells
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Insulin surge shifting phosphate, K+ and Mg2+ into cells
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs when a carbohydrate load triggers an insulin surge causing a rapid intracellular shift of phosphate, K+ and Mg2+, with expanding ECF volume and a spike in thiamine demand.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which is the cardinal electrolyte abnormality of refeeding syndrome?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Hypophosphataemia
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Low phosphate is the cardinal abnormality in refeeding syndrome (alongside low K+ and Mg2+), with consequences including cardiac and respiratory failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, coma and Wernicke's encephalopathy.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which single criterion alone makes a patient high-risk for refeeding syndrome (NICE)?
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: BMI <16
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Any one of BMI <16, weight loss >15% in 3–6 months, little/no intake >10 days, or low K+/PO4/Mg2+ before feeding is sufficient alone; two of BMI <18.5, weight loss >10%, little/no intake >5 days, or alcohol/drug history are needed otherwise.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: At what rate should feeding start in a patient at high risk of refeeding syndrome (NICE)?
options: Nil by mouth for a further 7 days first
Maximum 10 kcal/kg/day, building up over 4–7 days
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Maximum 10 kcal/kg/day, building up over 4–7 days
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: High-risk patients start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg in extreme cases, BMI <14), building to full needs over 4–7 days.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What thiamine regimen is recommended in refeeding-risk patients (NICE)?
options: Thiamine only if the patient has a seizure
Thiamine 1 g daily for the next 30 days
Thiamine 200–300 mg/day before and during feeding
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Thiamine 200–300 mg/day before and during feeding
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Thiamine 200–300 mg/day plus vitamin B co strong is given before and during the first 10 days of feeding in refeeding-risk patients.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How should electrolytes be managed when starting feeding in a refeeding-risk patient (NICE)?
options: Fully normalise all electrolytes before any feeding
Correct the electrolytes only after 10 days
Replace as needed, without delaying feeding
Give high-dose phosphate prophylactically to everyone
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Replace as needed, without delaying feeding
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Electrolytes (K+, PO4, Mg2+) are replaced as needed, but feeding is not delayed to pre-correct them before starting.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How should an enteral feeding tube be managed to prevent blockage?
options: Flush with water before and after every use
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Flush with water before and after every use
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: To prevent blockage, the tube is flushed with water before and after every use; feed sets are discarded every 24 h to prevent infection.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How should a patient be positioned to minimise aspiration during enteral feeding?
options: Nursed prone during and after feeding
Sitting fully upright only after the feed
Lying completely flat throughout the feed
Nursed at 30° or more during and after feeding
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Nursed at 30° or more during and after feeding
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: To minimise aspiration, patients are nursed at ≥30° during and after feeding, with post-pyloric tubes used for patients who must lie flat.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which bloods are monitored daily until stable during nutritional support?
options: U&Es, glucose, Mg, phosphate, LFTs and CRP
A full blood count and nothing else
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: U&Es, glucose, Mg, phosphate, LFTs and CRP
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Bloods monitored daily until stable include U&Es, glucose, Mg, phosphate, LFTs/INR, calcium, albumin and CRP; trace elements (Zn, Cu, Se) are checked periodically on long-term PN.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: How is clinically assisted nutrition and hydration (CANH) classified ethically, and what governs decisions about it?
options: Basic care requiring no consent at all
Basic care that can never be withdrawn
A medical treatment, with capacity driving it
A treatment that must always be continued
A treatment decided solely by the family
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: A medical treatment, with capacity driving it
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: CANH is a medical treatment, not basic care, and can be withheld or withdrawn using the same consent framework; capacity drives the decision, a competent patient's refusal must be respected, and if capacity is lacking the decision is made in best interests.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: Which four abilities define capacity under the Mental Capacity Act?
options: Understand, retain, weigh, communicate the decision
Read, write, sign, witness the decision
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Understand, retain, weigh, communicate the decision
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: Capacity requires the patient to understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: What did the Montgomery ruling change about consent?
options: Consent may be obtained by any member of staff
The Bolam standard was reinstated for consent
Patients must be told all material risks
Verbal consent is sufficient for all procedures
Only risks greater than 1% need to be disclosed
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Patients must be told all material risks
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.explanation: The Montgomery ruling requires disclosure of all material risks a reasonable patient would want to know, or that this specific patient would consider significant, replacing the old Bolam standard for consent.

conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.question: A patient lacking capacity needs emergency surgery. How should consent proceed?
options: Cancel the operation until capacity returns
Proceed in best interests, document, consider an IMCA
Obtain legally binding consent from next of kin
Wait for a court order before any treatment
Delay until capacity returns regardless of urgency
conditions__ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRI.answer: Proceed in best interests, document, consider an IMCA
